**Kansas City**, abbreviated **KC** or **KCMO**, is the largest city in the U.S. state of [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri") by both [population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Missouri "List of cities in Missouri") and area. It is located on the [Missouri River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River") at its confluence with the [Kansas River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_River "Kansas River"), within [Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County,_Missouri "Jackson County, Missouri"), [Clay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clay_County,_Missouri "Clay County, Missouri"), [Platte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platte_County,_Missouri "Platte County, Missouri") and [Cass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_Missouri "Cass County, Missouri") counties. It is the [37th-most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_cities_by_population "List of United States cities by population") in the United States and sixth-most populous city in the [Midwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwest "Midwest"), with a population of 508,090 at the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-QuickFacts-3)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-10) The [Kansas City metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_metropolitan_area "Kansas City metropolitan area"), which straddles the Missouri–[Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas") state line, is the [31st-most populous metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_statistical_area "Metropolitan statistical area") in the nation, at 2.25 million residents.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-13)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-2020Pop-5)

Kansas City was founded in the 1830s as a port on the Missouri and Kansas rivers. On June 1, 1850, the town of Kansas was incorporated; soon afterwards, a region designated as the [Kansas Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_Territory "Kansas Territory") was established. Confusion between the city and the territory of Kansas ensued, so the name Kansas City was assigned to distinguish the city from the territory. The city's growth was closely tied to [westward expansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territorial_evolution_of_the_United_States "Territorial evolution of the United States"), as railroads and the [Kansas City Stockyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Stockyards "Kansas City Stockyards") established it as a major transportation and livestock center.

Situated along Missouri's western border with Kansas, Kansas City encompasses 319.03 square miles (826.3 km 2), making it the [25th-largest U.S. city by area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_cities_by_area "List of United States cities by area"). It is one of the two county seats of Jackson County, alongside [Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence,_Missouri "Independence, Missouri"). The city is known for landmarks and districts including the [River Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Market,_Kansas_City "River Market, Kansas City"), [18th and Vine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_and_Vine "18th and Vine"), and [Country Club Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Club_Plaza "Country Club Plaza"). It is internationally recognized for [Kansas City jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_jazz "Kansas City jazz"), its [extensive system of fountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Fountains "City of Fountains"), the [Kansas City Chiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Chiefs "Kansas City Chiefs") and [Kansas City Royals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Royals "Kansas City Royals") sports franchises, and regional cuisine including [Kansas City-style barbecue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City-style_barbecue "Kansas City-style barbecue") and [strip steak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strip_steak "Strip steak").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [History of the Kansas City metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Kansas_City_metropolitan_area "History of the Kansas City metropolitan area")

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Kansas_City,_Missouri "Timeline of Kansas City, Missouri").

The town of [Kansas, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas,_Missouri "Kansas, Missouri"), was incorporated on June 1, 1850, reincorporated and renamed "City of Kansas" on March 28, 1853, and renamed "Kansas City" in 1889. The [Kansas City metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_metropolitan_area "Kansas City metropolitan area") straddles the border between Missouri and Kansas at [Kaw Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaw_Point "Kaw Point"), and was considered a good place to settle. The [Antioch Christian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioch_Christian_Church_(Kansas_City,_Missouri) "Antioch Christian Church (Kansas City, Missouri)"), [Dr. James Compton House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._James_Compton_House "Dr. James Compton House"), and [Woodneath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodneath "Woodneath") are listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-14)

### Indigenous peoples and settlement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Indigenous peoples and settlement")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Westport_Pioneers_Statue.jpg/250px-Westport_Pioneers_Statue.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Westport_Pioneers_Statue.jpg)

The Kansas City Pioneer Square monument in Westport features [Pony Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pony_Express "Pony Express") founder [Alexander Majors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Majors "Alexander Majors"), Westport and Kansas City founder [John Calvin McCoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin_McCoy "John Calvin McCoy"), and [mountain man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_man "Mountain man")[Jim Bridger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Bridger "Jim Bridger") who owned Chouteau's Store.

In past centuries, the area's tribal inhabitants include the [Hopewell tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopewell_tradition "Hopewell tradition"), [Mississippian culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippian_culture "Mississippian culture"), [Kansa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaw_people "Kaw people"), [Osage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osage_Nation "Osage Nation"), [Otoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otoe "Otoe"), and [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouria "Missouria").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-15) The first documented European visitor to the eventual site of Kansas City was French military officer [Étienne de Veniard, Sieur de Bourgmont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tienne_de_Veniard,_Sieur_de_Bourgmont "Étienne de Veniard, Sieur de Bourgmont"), who was also the first European to explore the lower Missouri River. Criticized for his response to the [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American "Native American") attack on [Fort Détroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_D%C3%A9troit "Fort Détroit"), he had deserted his post as fort commander and was avoiding French authorities. Bourgmont lived with a Native American wife in a village about 90 miles (140 km) east near [Brunswick, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunswick,_Missouri "Brunswick, Missouri"), where he illegally traded [furs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Furs "Furs").

To clear his name, he wrote _Exact Description of Louisiana, of Its Harbors, Lands and Rivers, and Names of the Indian Tribes That Occupy It, and the Commerce and Advantages to Be Derived Therefrom for the Establishment of a Colony_ in 1713 and _The Route to Be Taken to Ascend the Missouri River_ in 1714. In the documents, he describes the junction of the "Grande Riv[ière] des Cansez" and Missouri River, as the first adoption of those names. French cartographer [Guillaume Delisle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Delisle "Guillaume Delisle") used the descriptions to make the area's first reasonably accurate map.

The [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Spain "Kingdom of Spain") took over the region in the [Treaty of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_(1763) "Treaty of Paris (1763)") in 1763, but were not to play a major role other than taxing and licensing Missouri River ship traffic. The French continued their [fur trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_trade "Fur trade") under Spanish license, before [France reclaimed the territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Treaty_of_San_Ildefonso "Third Treaty of San Ildefonso") in 1800. Then, after the 1803 [Louisiana Purchase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Purchase "Louisiana Purchase"), explorers [Lewis and Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_and_Clark "Lewis and Clark") visited the [confluence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confluence "Confluence") of the Kansas and Missouri rivers on their way to the Pacific West, in June 1804, and on their return, in September 1806. Clark noted it had "a Commanding Situation" to build a fort[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-16).

In 1821, the French [Chouteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chouteau "Chouteau") fur-trading family, active in [St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis") as early as 1765, reached the location of what would become Kansas City. There, [François Chouteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Chouteau "François Chouteau") established a trading post consisting of warehouses and dwellings, dubbed "Chouteau's Landing", the first permanent settlement of the site[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-17). The settlement changed locations several times due to floods but the Chouteau family, along with the French Canadian trappers, traders and voyageurs that had come with them, remained in the area[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-18).

With successive treaties and the 1830 national [Indian Removal Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Removal_Act "Indian Removal Act"), tribes originally living in Missouri were progressively forced to move west, to Kansas and further, accelerating the settlement of the Kansas City area by whites[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-20).

In 1831, a group of [Mormons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mormons "Mormons") from [New York state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_state "New York state") led by [Joseph Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Smith "Joseph Smith") settled in the area. They built the first school within what became Kansas City, but were forced out by [mob violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mob_violence "Mob violence") in 1833.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-21) In 1831, Gabriel Prudhomme Sr., a Canadian trapper and partner of François Chouteau, purchased 257 acres (104 ha) fronting the Missouri River. He established a home for his wife, Josephine, and six children, and operated a ferry on the river.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-22)

In 1833, [John Calvin McCoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin_McCoy "John Calvin McCoy"), son of Baptist missionary [Isaac McCoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_McCoy "Isaac McCoy") and brother-in-law of [Johnston Lykins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnston_Lykins "Johnston Lykins"), established [West Port](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westport,_Kansas_City "Westport, Kansas City") along the [Santa Fe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe_Trail "Santa Fe Trail"), [Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Trail "Oregon Trail") and [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Trail "California Trail") trails, three miles (4.8 kilometers) south of the river. In 1834, McCoy established Westport Landing on a rocky ledge situated on a bend in the Missouri, to serve as a landing point for West Port, with Lykins as the first postmaster. He found it more convenient to have his goods offloaded at the Prudhomme landing, next to Chouteau's landing, than in Independence. Following the same route as emigrants and gold seekers headed toward the Pacific Coast, Sante Fe traders shipped goods up the Missouri river by steamboat to Westport before continuing West by land.

On the year of Gabriel Prudhomme's death, a group of fourteen investors purchased his land at auction on November 14, 1838, for $4,220[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-23). By 1839, the investors divided the property and the first lots were sold in 1846, after legal complications were settled. The remaining lots were sold by February 1850.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Founding and westward expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Founding and westward expansion")]

See also: [Bleeding Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleeding_Kansas "Bleeding Kansas") and [History of slavery in Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_slavery_in_Missouri "History of slavery in Missouri")

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Kansas_City_in_1843%2C_drawing_from_Centennial_History_of_Oregon.png/250px-Kansas_City_in_1843%2C_drawing_from_Centennial_History_of_Oregon.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kansas_City_in_1843,_drawing_from_Centennial_History_of_Oregon.png)

In 1843, Kansas City was depicted in a history of [Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon "Oregon").

On June 3, 1850, the landing area was incorporated as the town of [Kansas, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas,_Missouri "Kansas, Missouri"), named after the nearby native tribe[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-24). By that time, the towns of Kansas, Westport, and nearby [Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence,_Missouri "Independence, Missouri"), had become critical points in the [westward expansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westward_expansion "Westward expansion") of the United States. Three major [trails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_roads_and_trails_of_the_United_States "Historical roads and trails of the United States") – the Santa Fe, California, and Oregon – all passed through Jackson County.

On February 22, 1853, Kansas was reincorporated and renamed the City of Kansas with its first elected mayor, [William Samuel Gregory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Samuel_Gregory "William Samuel Gregory"). Due to a legal discovery of living outside city boundaries, he was soon succeeded by Johnston Lykins as the second (but first legally elected) mayor.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-26) The city had an area of 0.70 square miles (1.8 km 2) and a population of 2,500. The boundary lines extended from the middle of the Missouri River south to what is now Ninth Street, and from Bluff Street on the west to a point between Holmes Road and Charlotte Street on the east.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-27)

During the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), the city and its immediate surroundings were the focus of intense military activity. Although the [First Battle of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Battle_of_Independence "First Battle of Independence") in August 1862 resulted in a [Confederate States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_Army "Confederate States Army") victory, the Confederates were unable to leverage their win in any significant fashion, as Kansas City was occupied by Union troops and proved too heavily fortified to assault. The [Second Battle of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Independence "Second Battle of Independence"), which occurred on October 21–22, 1864, as part of [Sterling Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sterling_Price "Sterling Price")'s [Missouri expedition of 1864](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price's_Raid "Price's Raid"), also resulted in a Confederate triumph. Once again their victory proved hollow, as Price was decisively defeated in the pivotal [Battle of Westport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Westport "Battle of Westport") the next day, effectively ending Confederate efforts to regain Missouri.

General [Thomas Ewing, Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Ewing,_Jr. "Thomas Ewing, Jr."), in response to a successful raid on nearby [Lawrence, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence,_Kansas "Lawrence, Kansas"), led by [William Quantrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Quantrill "William Quantrill"), issued [General Order No. 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Order_No._11_(1863) "General Order No. 11 (1863)"), forcing the eviction of residents in four western Missouri counties – including Jackson – except those living in the city and nearby communities and those whose allegiance to the Union was certified by Ewing.

### Late 19th and early 20th centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Late 19th and early 20th centuries")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Junction_of_Main_and_Delaware_Streets%2C_Kansas_City%2C_Mo_%28NYPL_b12647398-68704%29.tiff/lossy-page1-250px-Junction_of_Main_and_Delaware_Streets%2C_Kansas_City%2C_Mo_%28NYPL_b12647398-68704%29.tiff.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Junction_of_Main_and_Delaware_Streets,_Kansas_City,_Mo_(NYPL_b12647398-68704).tiff)

The junction of Main and Delaware Streets in 1898

After the Civil War, Kansas City grew rapidly. The selection of the city over [Leavenworth, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leavenworth,_Kansas "Leavenworth, Kansas"), for the [Hannibal and St. Joseph Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal_and_St._Joseph_Railroad "Hannibal and St. Joseph Railroad") bridge over the [Missouri River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River") brought significant growth. The population exploding after 1869, when Hannibal Bridge, designed by [Octave Chanute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave_Chanute "Octave Chanute"), opened. The boom prompted a name change to Kansas City in 1889, and the city limits to be extended south and east. Westport became part of Kansas City on December 2, 1897. In 1900, Kansas City was the 22nd largest city in the country, with a population of 163,752 residents.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-U.S._Census_Bureau-28)

[Landscape architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landscape_architecture "Landscape architecture")[George Kessler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Kessler "George Kessler") shaped Kansas City into a leading example of the [City Beautiful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Beautiful "City Beautiful") movement, with a network of boulevards and parks.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-29) New neighborhoods like [Southmoreland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southmoreland "Southmoreland") and the Rockhill District were conceived to accommodate the city's largest residencies of palatial proportions.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The obsolescence of [Union Depot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Union_Station#Union_Depot_era "Kansas City Union Station") in West Bottoms in favor of the new [Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Union_Station "Kansas City Union Station") in 1914, and the opening of the [Liberty Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Memorial "Liberty Memorial") in 1923, provided two of the city's most identifiable landmarks. [Robert A. Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_A._Long "Robert A. Long"), president of the Liberty Memorial Association, was a driving force in the funding for construction. Long was a longtime resident and wealthy businessman. He built the [R. A. Long Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._A._Long_Building "R. A. Long Building") for the [Long-Bell Lumber Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-Bell_Lumber_Company "Long-Bell Lumber Company"), his home, [Corinthian Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Museum "Kansas City Museum") (now the [Kansas City Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Museum "Kansas City Museum")) and [Longview Farm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longview_Farm "Longview Farm").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-30) Further spurring Kansas City's growth was the opening of the innovative [Country Club Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Club_Plaza "Country Club Plaza") development by [J. C. Nichols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._C._Nichols "J. C. Nichols") in 1925, as part of his [Country Club District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Club_District "Country Club District") plan.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1911, [Elias Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Disney "Elias Disney") moved [his family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney_family "Disney family") from [Marceline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marceline,_Missouri "Marceline, Missouri") to Kansas City. They lived in a new home at 3028 Bellefontaine with a garage he built, in which [Walt Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney "Walt Disney") made his first [animation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animation "Animation").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-31) In 1919, Walt returned from France where he had served as a [Red Cross ambulance driver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambulance_drivers_during_World_War_I "List of ambulance drivers during World War I") in [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). He started the first animation company in Kansas City, [Laugh-O-Gram Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laugh-O-Gram_Studio "Laugh-O-Gram Studio"), in which he designed [Mickey Mouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mickey_Mouse "Mickey Mouse"). When the company went bankrupt, Walt Disney moved to [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles") and started [The Walt Disney Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company") on October 16, 1923.

[The Kansas City streetcar system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetcars_in_Kansas_City "Streetcars in Kansas City") once had hundreds of miles of streetcars running through the city and was one of the largest systems in the country.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-32) In 1903 the 8th Street Tunnel was built as an underground streetcar system through the city. The last run of the streetcar was on June 23, 1957, but the tunnel still exists.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-33)

#### Pendergast political machine

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Pendergast political machine")]

At the start of the 20th century, [political machines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_machines "Political machines") gained clout in the city, with the one led by [Tom Pendergast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Pendergast "Tom Pendergast") dominating the city by 1925. Several important buildings and structures were built during this time, including the [Kansas City City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_City_Hall "Kansas City City Hall") and the Jackson County Courthouse. During this time, he aided one of his nephew's friends, [Harry S. Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman "Harry S. Truman"), in a political career. Truman eventually became a senator, then vice president, then [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Harry_S._Truman "Presidency of Harry S. Truman").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-34) The machine fell in 1939 when Pendergast, riddled with health problems, pleaded guilty to tax evasion after long federal investigations. His biographers have summed up his uniqueness:

> Pendergast may bear comparison to various big-city bosses, but his open alliance with hardened criminals, his cynical subversion of the democratic process, his monarchistic style of living, his increasingly insatiable gambling habit, his grasping for a business empire, and his promotion of Kansas City as a wide-open town with every kind of vice imaginable, combined with his professed compassion for the poor and very real role as city builder, made him bigger than life, difficult to characterize.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-35)

### Mid- to late 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Mid- to late 20th century")]

[Troost Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troost_Avenue "Troost Avenue") was once the eastern edge of Kansas City, Missouri and a residential corridor nicknamed Millionaire Row. It is now widely seen as one of the city's most prominent racial and economic dividing lines due to urban decay, which was caused by [white flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_flight "White flight").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-37) During the civil rights era the city blocked people of color from moving to homes west of Troost Avenue, causing the areas east of Troost to have one of the worst murder rates in the country. This led to the dominating economic success of neighboring [Johnson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_County,_Kansas "Johnson County, Kansas").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-38)

In 1950, African Americans represented 12.2% of Kansas City's population.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-U.S._Census_Bureau-28) The city's most populous ethnic group, non-Hispanic whites,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-census1-39) declined from 89.5% in 1930 to 54.9% in 2010.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-U.S._Census_Bureau-28)

In 1940, the city had about 400,000 residents; by 2000, it had about 440,000. From 1940 to 1960, the city more than doubled its physical size, while increasing its population by only about 75,000. By 1970, the city covered approximately 316 square miles (820 km 2), more than five times its size in 1940.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Aggressively annexing the surrounding suburbs and undeveloped land spared Kansas City from the severe population loss suffered by cities like St. Louis and Detroit, similar cities which both lost over 50% of their population in the postwar era. In the most neglected neighborhoods, however, the same pattern of abandonment occurred and left behind massive numbers of vacant lots and abandoned homes, especially in the areas east of Troost.

The [Hyatt Regency walkway collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyatt_Regency_walkway_collapse "Hyatt Regency walkway collapse") was a major disaster that occurred on July 17, 1981, killing 114 people and injuring more than 200 others during a [tea dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_dance "Tea dance") in the 45-story [Hyatt Regency hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheraton_Kansas_City_Hotel_at_Crown_Center "Sheraton Kansas City Hotel at Crown Center") in [Crown Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Center "Crown Center"). It is the deadliest structural collapse in US history other than the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-40) In 2015 a memorial called the Skywalk Memorial Plaza was built for the families of the victims of the disaster, across the street from the hotel which is now a Sheraton.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-41)

### 21st century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 21st century")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Kansas_city_%2816778782291%29.jpg/250px-Kansas_city_%2816778782291%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kansas_city_(16778782291).jpg)

[Downtown Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Kansas_City "Downtown Kansas City") looking over [Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_(Kansas_City) "Union Station (Kansas City)") from the Liberty Memorial

In the 21st century, the Kansas City area has undergone extensive redevelopment, with more than $6 billion in improvements to the downtown area on the Missouri side. One of the main goals is to attract convention and tourist dollars, office workers, and residents to downtown KCMO. Among the projects include the redevelopment of the [Power & Light District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_&_Light_District "Power & Light District") into a retail and entertainment district; and the Sprint Center, an 18,500-seat arena that opened in 2007, funded by a 2004 ballot initiative involving a tax on car rentals and hotels, designed to meet the stadium specifications for a possible future NBA or NHL franchise,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-42) and was renamed [T-Mobile Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-Mobile_Center "T-Mobile Center") in 2020; Kemper Arena, which was functionally superseded by Sprint Center, fell into disrepair and was sold to private developers. By 2018, the arena was being converted to a sports complex under the name [Hy-Vee Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hy-Vee_Arena "Hy-Vee Arena").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-43) The Kauffman Performing Arts Center opened in 2011 providing a new, modern home to the KC Orchestra and Ballet. In 2015, an 800-room Hyatt Convention Center Hotel was announced for a site next to the Performance Arts Center & Bartle Hall. Construction was scheduled to start in early 2018 with Loews as the operator.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-44)

From 2007 to 2017, downtown residential population in Kansas City quadrupled and continues to grow. The area has grown from almost 4,000 residents in the early 2000s to nearly 30,000 as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit). Kansas City's downtown ranks as the sixth-fastest-growing downtown in America with the population expected to grow by more than 40% by 2022. Conversions of office buildings such as the Power & Light Building and the Commerce Bank Tower into residential and hotel space has helped to fulfill the demand. New apartment complexes like One, Two, and Three Lights, River Market West, and 503 Main have begun to reshape Kansas City's skyline. Strong demand has led to occupancy rates in the upper 90%.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-45)

The residential population of downtown has boomed, and the office population has dropped significantly from the early 2000s to the mid-2010s. Top employers like AMC moved their operations to modern office buildings in the suburbs. High office vacancy plagued downtown, leading to the neglect of many office buildings. By the mid-2010s, many office buildings were converted to residential uses and the Class A vacancy rate plunged to 12% in 2017. Swiss Re, Virgin Mobile, AutoAlert, and others have begun to move operations to downtown Kansas City from the suburbs and expensive coastal cities.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-47)

The area has seen additional development through various transportation projects, including improvements to the [Grandview Triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandview_Triangle "Grandview Triangle"), which intersects Interstates 435 and 470, and [U.S. Route 71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_71_(Missouri) "U.S. Route 71 (Missouri)"). In July 2005, the [Kansas City Area Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Area_Transportation_Authority "Kansas City Area Transportation Authority") (KCATA) launched Kansas City's first [bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") line, the [Metro Area Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Area_Express "Metro Area Express") (MAX), which links the River Market, downtown, Union Station, Crown Center and the Country Club Plaza. The KCATA continues to expand MAX with additional routes on Prospect Avenue, Troost Avenue, and Independence Avenue.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-48)

In 2013, construction began on a two-mile [streetcar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KC_Streetcar "KC Streetcar") line in downtown Kansas City (funded by a $102 million ballot initiative that was passed in 2012) that runs between the River Market and Union Station, it began operation in May 2016. In 2017, voters approved the formation of a TDD to expand the streetcar line south 3.5 miles from Union Station to UMKC's Volker Campus. Additionally in 2017, the KC Port Authority began engineering studies for a Port Authority funded streetcar expansion north to Berkley Riverfront Park. Citywide, voter support for rail projects continues to grow with numerous light rail projects in the works.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-50)

In 2016, Jackson County, Missouri, acquired unused rail lines as part of a long-term commuter rail plan. For the time being, the line is being converted to a trail while county officials negotiate with railroads for access to tracks in downtown Kansas City. On November 7, 2017, Kansas City voters overwhelmingly approved a new single terminal at [Kansas City International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_International_Airport "Kansas City International Airport") by a 75% to 25% margin. The new single terminal replaced the three existing "Clover Leafs" at KCI Airport on February 28, 2023.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Kansas_City_by_Sentinel-2.jpg/250px-Kansas_City_by_Sentinel-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kansas_City_by_Sentinel-2.jpg)

The Kansas City metropolitan area was photographed by the [Sentinel-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentinel-2 "Sentinel-2") satellite in July 2022.

The city has an area of 319.03 square miles (826.28 km 2), of which, 314.95 square miles (815.72 km 2) is land and 4.08 square miles (10.57 km 2) is water.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-51) Bluffs overlook the rivers and river bottom areas. Kansas City proper is bowl-shaped and is surrounded to the north and south by [glacier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacier "Glacier")-carved [limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone "Limestone") and [bedrock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedrock "Bedrock") cliffs. Kansas City is at the confluence between the Dakota and Minnesota ice lobes during the maximum late Independence glaciation of the [Pleistocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleistocene "Pleistocene")[epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geologic_time_scale "Geologic time scale"). The Kansas and Missouri rivers cut wide valleys into the terrain when the glaciers melted and drained. A partially filled spillway valley crosses the central city. This valley is an eastward continuation of the Turkey Creek Valley. It is the closest major city to the geographic center of the contiguous United States, or "Lower 48".

#### Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Architecture")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Community_Christian_Church_KCMO.jpg/250px-Community_Christian_Church_KCMO.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Community_Christian_Church_KCMO.jpg)

[Community Christian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_Christian_Church_(Kansas_City,_Missouri) "Community Christian Church (Kansas City, Missouri)") was designed by [Frank Lloyd Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lloyd_Wright "Frank Lloyd Wright") and is next to the [Country Club Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Club_Plaza "Country Club Plaza").

Main article: [Architecture of Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture_of_Kansas_City "Architecture of Kansas City")

Further information: [List of fountains in the Kansas City metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fountains_in_the_Kansas_City_metropolitan_area "List of fountains in the Kansas City metropolitan area") and [List of tallest buildings in Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_in_Kansas_City,_Missouri "List of tallest buildings in Kansas City, Missouri")

The [Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson-Atkins_Museum_of_Art "Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art") opened its Euro-Style Bloch addition in 2007, and the Safdie-designed [Kauffman Center for the Performing Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kauffman_Center_for_the_Performing_Arts "Kauffman Center for the Performing Arts") opened in 2011. The [Power and Light Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Power_and_Light_Building "Kansas City Power and Light Building") is influenced by the [Art Deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Deco "Art Deco") style and sports a glowing sky beacon. The new world headquarters of [H&R Block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H&R_Block "H&R Block") is a 20-story all-glass oval bathed in a soft green light. The four industrial artworks atop the support towers of the Kansas City Convention Center ([Bartle Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartle_Hall "Bartle Hall")) were once the subject of ridicule, but now define the night skyline near the [T-Mobile Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-Mobile_Center "T-Mobile Center") along with [One Kansas City Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Kansas_City_Place "One Kansas City Place") (Missouri's tallest office tower), the [KCTV-Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KCTV-Tower "KCTV-Tower") (Missouri's tallest freestanding structure) and the [Liberty Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Memorial "Liberty Memorial"), a World War I memorial and museum that flaunts simulated flames and smoke billowing into the night skyline. It was designated as the [National World War I Museum and Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_World_War_I_Museum_and_Memorial "National World War I Museum and Memorial") in 2004 by the United States Congress. Kansas City is home to significant national and international architecture firms including ACI Boland, [BNIM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BNIM "BNIM"), [360 Architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/360_Architecture "360 Architecture"), [HNTB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HNTB "HNTB"), [Populous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Populous_(architects) "Populous (architects)"). [Frank Lloyd Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lloyd_Wright "Frank Lloyd Wright") designed two private residences and [Community Christian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_Christian_Church_(Kansas_City,_Missouri) "Community Christian Church (Kansas City, Missouri)") there.

Kansas City hosts more than 200 working fountains, especially on the Country Club Plaza. Designs range from French-inspired traditional to modern. Highlights include the Black Marble H&R Block fountain in front of Union Station, which features synchronized water jets; the Nichols Bronze Horses at the corner of Main and J.C. Nichols Parkway at the entrance to the Plaza Shopping District; and the fountain at [Hallmark Cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallmark_Cards "Hallmark Cards") World Headquarters in [Crown Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Center "Crown Center").

#### City Market

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: City Market")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/BridgeTownofKansas.jpg/250px-BridgeTownofKansas.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BridgeTownofKansas.jpg)

The [Town of Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_of_Kansas "Town of Kansas") Bridge connects pedestrian traffic from the Riverfront Heritage Trail (starting at Berkley Riverfront Park) to River Market.

Since its inception in 1857, [City Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Market,_Kansas_City "River Market, Kansas City") has been one of the largest and most enduring public farmers' markets in the American Midwest, linking growers and small businesses to the community. More than 30 full-time merchants operate year-round and offer specialty foods, fresh meats and seafood, restaurants and cafes, floral, and home accessories.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-Thecitymarket.org-53) The City Market has the [Arabia Steamboat Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabia_Steamboat_Museum "Arabia Steamboat Museum"), which houses artifacts from a steamboat that sank near Kansas City in 1856.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-Thecitymarket.org-53)

#### Downtown

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Downtown")]

Main article: [Downtown Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Kansas_City "Downtown Kansas City")

[Downtown Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Kansas_City "Downtown Kansas City") is 2.9 square miles (7.5 km 2) bounded by the Missouri River to the north, 31st Street to the south, [Troost Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troost_Avenue "Troost Avenue") to the east, and State Line Road to the west. Areas near Downtown Kansas City include the [39th Street District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/39th_Street_(Kansas_City) "39th Street (Kansas City)"), which is known as Restaurant Row,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-54) and features one of Kansas City's largest selections of independently owned restaurants and boutique shops. It is a center of literary and visual arts, and [bohemian culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemian_culture "Bohemian culture"). [Crown Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Center "Crown Center") is the headquarters of [Hallmark Cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallmark_Cards "Hallmark Cards") and a major downtown shopping and entertainment complex. It is connected to Union Station by a series of covered walkways. The [Country Club Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Club_Plaza "Country Club Plaza"), or "the Plaza", is an upscale, outdoor shopping, and entertainment district. It is the first suburban shopping district in the United States,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-55) designed to accommodate shoppers arriving by automobile,[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-56) and is surrounded by apartments and condominiums, including several high rise buildings. The associated [Country Club District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Club_District "Country Club District") to the south includes the Sunset Hill and [Brookside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookside_(Kansas_City) "Brookside (Kansas City)") neighborhoods, and is traversed by [Ward Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ward_Parkway "Ward Parkway"), a landscaped boulevard known for its statuary, fountains, and large, historic homes. [Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_(Kansas_City) "Union Station (Kansas City)") is home to [Science City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_City_at_Union_Station "Science City at Union Station"), restaurants, shopping, theaters, and the city's [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak") facility.

After years of neglect and seas of parking lots, Downtown Kansas City is undergoing a period of change with over $6 billion in development since 2000. Many residential properties recently have been or are under redevelopment in three surrounding warehouse loft districts and the Central Business District. The [Power & Light District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_&_Light_District "Power & Light District"), a new, nine-block entertainment district comprising numerous restaurants, bars, and retail shops, was developed by the [Cordish Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordish_Company "Cordish Company") of [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"). Its first tenant opened on November 9, 2007. It is anchored by the [T-Mobile Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-Mobile_Center "T-Mobile Center"), a 19,000-seat sports and entertainment complex.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-57)

Kansas City is in the [Midwestern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwestern_United_States "Midwestern United States"), near the geographic center of the country, at the confluence of the [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River") and [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_River "Kansas River") rivers. The city lies in either the [humid continental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental "Humid continental") zone when using the 32°F (0°C) isotherm, or in the [humid subtropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_subtropical "Humid subtropical") zone when using the 27°F (−3°C) isotherm.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-58) The city experiences roughly 104 air frosts on average per annum.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-59)[_[unreliable source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable\_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")_] The city is part of USDA plant [hardiness zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardiness_zone "Hardiness zone") 5b and 6a.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-60) In the center of North America, far removed from a significant body of water, there is significant potential for extreme hot and cold swings throughout the year. The warmest month is July, with a 24-hour average temperature of 81.0°F (27.2°C). The summer months are hot and humid, with moist air riding up from the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico"), and high temperatures surpass 100°F (38°C) on 5.6 days of the year, and 90°F (32°C) on 47 days.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-NWS_Pleasant_Hill,_MO-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-62) The coldest month of the year is January, with an average temperature of 31.0°F (−0.6°C). Winters are cold, with 22 days where the high temperature is at or below 32°F (0°C) and 2.5 nights with a low at or below 0°F (−18°C).[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-NWS_Pleasant_Hill,_MO-61) The official record highest temperature is 113°F (45°C), set on August 14, 1936, at Downtown Airport, while the official record lowest is −23°F (−31°C), set on December 22 and 23, 1989.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-NWS_Pleasant_Hill,_MO-61) Normal seasonal snowfall is 13.4 inches (34 cm) at Downtown Airport and 18.8 in (48 cm) at Kansas City International Airport. The average window for freezing temperatures is October 31 to April 4, while for measurable (0.1 in or 0.25 cm) snowfall, it is November 27 to March 16 as measured at Kansas City International Airport.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-NWS_Pleasant_Hill,_MO-61) Precipitation, both in frequency and total accumulation, shows a marked uptick in late spring and summer.

Kansas City is located in [Tornado Alley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_Alley "Tornado Alley"), a broad region where cold air from [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada") collides with warm air from the Gulf of Mexico, leading to the formation of powerful storms, especially during the spring. The Kansas City metropolitan area has experienced several significant outbreaks of [tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado") in the past, including the [1957 Ruskin Heights tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1957_Ruskin_Heights_tornado "1957 Ruskin Heights tornado"),[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-63) the [2019 Lawrence–Linwood tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Lawrence%E2%80%93Linwood_tornado "2019 Lawrence–Linwood tornado") and the [May 2003 tornado outbreak sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_2003_tornado_outbreak_sequence "May 2003 tornado outbreak sequence"). The region can also experience [ice storms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_storm "Ice storm") during the winter, such as the [2002 ice storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Central_Plains_Ice_Storm "2002 Central Plains Ice Storm") during which hundreds of thousands of residents lost power for days or weeks.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-64) Kansas City and its outlying areas are also subject to flooding, including the Great Floods of [1844](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Flood_of_1844 "Great Flood of 1844"), [1951](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Flood_of_1951 "Great Flood of 1951"), and [1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Flood_of_1993 "Great Flood of 1993").

The Latino/Hispanic population of Kansas City, which is heavily Mexican and [Central American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America"), is spread throughout the metropolitan area, with some concentration in the northeast part of the city and southwest of downtown. The Asian population, mostly Southeast Asian, is partly concentrated within the northeast side to the Columbus Park neighborhood in the Greater Downtown area, a historically [Italian American neighborhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Italian_American_neighborhoods "List of Italian American neighborhoods"), the UMKC area and in River Market, in northern Kansas City.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-73)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-74)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-75)

The historic (pre-World War II) city of Kansas City contains roughly 58 square miles (150 km 2) and has a population density of about 5,000 inhabitants per square mile (1,900/km 2). Its borders are the Missouri River on the north (save for a small community named [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallatin_Township,_Clay_County,_Missouri#Settlements "Gallatin Township, Clay County, Missouri") and [Charles B. Wheeler Downtown Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_B._Wheeler_Downtown_Airport "Charles B. Wheeler Downtown Airport") on the river's north bank), 79th Street on the south, the Blue River on the east, and State Line Road on the west. From the 1950s to the 1970s, Kansas City annexed large amounts of land, most of which remain largely undeveloped.

Between the 2000 and 2010 census counts, the urban core of Kansas City continued to drop significantly in population. The areas of Greater Downtown in the center city, and sections near I-435 and I-470 in the south, and Highway 152 in the north are the only areas of Kansas City, Missouri, to have an increase in population, with the Northland population growing the most.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-76) Even so, the population of Kansas City as a whole from 2000 to 2010 increased by 4.1%.

### Irish-American community

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kansas_City,_Missouri&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Irish-American community")]

In 2021, the US Census Bureau estimated 253,040 people of Irish descent in the metro, with 123,934 in Jackson, Clay, and Platte Counties.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-91) The Irish were the first large immigrant group to settle in Kansas City following the lead of [Fr. Bernard Donnelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Donnelly "Bernard Donnelly") (c.1800–1880) and founded its first newspaper.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-92) The Irish community includes bands, dancers, Irish stores, newspapers, and the [Kansas City Irish Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Irish_Center "Kansas City Irish Center") at Drexel Hall in Midtown. The first book detailing Irish history in Kansas City is _Missouri Irish: Irish Settlers on the American Frontier_, published in 1984. The Kansas City Irish Fest is held over Labor Day weekend in Crown Center and Washington Park.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-93)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri#cite_note-94)

Minneapolis[b] is a city in Hennepin County, Minnesota, United States, and its county seat.[4] With a population of 429,954 as of the 2020 census, it is the state's most populous city.[8] Located in the state's center near the eastern border, it occupies both banks of the Upper Mississippi River and adjoins Saint Paul, the state capital of Minnesota. Minneapolis, Saint Paul, and the surrounding area are collectively known as the Twin Cities, a metropolitan area with 3.69 million residents.[14] Minneapolis is built on an artesian aquifer on relatively flat terrain and is known for cold, snowy winters and hot, humid summers. Nicknamed the "City of Lakes",[15] Minneapolis is abundant in water, with thirteen lakes, wetlands, the Mississippi River, creeks, and waterfalls. The city's public park system is connected by the Grand Rounds National Scenic Byway.

Dakota people previously inhabited the site of today's Minneapolis. European settlement began north of Fort Snelling along Saint Anthony Falls—the only natural waterfall on the Mississippi River.[16] Location near the fort and the falls' power—with its potential for industrial activity—fostered the city's early growth. For a time in the 19th century, Minneapolis was the lumber and flour milling capital of the world, and as home to the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, it has preserved its financial clout into the 21st century. A Minneapolis Depression-era labor strike brought about federal worker protections. Work in Minneapolis contributed to the computing industry, and the city is the birthplace of General Mills, the Pillsbury brand, Target Corporation, and Thermo King mobile refrigeration.

The city's major arts institutions include the Minneapolis Institute of Art, the Walker Art Center, the Minnesota Orchestra, and the Guthrie Theater. Four professional sports teams play downtown. Musician Prince played at the First Avenue nightclub. Minneapolis is home to the University of Minnesota's main campus. The city's public transport is provided by Metro Transit, and the international airport, serving the Twin Cities region, is located towards the south on the city limits.

Residents adhere to more than fifty religions. Despite its well-regarded quality of life,[17] Minneapolis has stark disparities among its residents—arguably the most critical issue confronting the city in the 21st century.[18] Governed by a mayor-council system, Minneapolis has a political landscape dominated by the Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party (DFL), with Jacob Frey serving as mayor since 2018.

Historyedit
Main article: History of Minneapolis
Dakota homelandedit
Further information: Dakota people, Ojibwe, Bdóte, and Dakota War of 1862

Two Indigenous nations inhabited the area now called Minneapolis.[19] Archaeologists have evidence that since 1000 AD,[20] they were the Dakota (one half of the Sioux nation),[21] and, after the 1700s,[22] the Ojibwe (also known as Chippewa, members of the Anishinaabe nations).[23] Dakota people have different stories to explain their creation.[24] One widely accepted story says the Dakota emerged from Bdóte,[24] the confluence of the Minnesota and Mississippi rivers. Dakota are the only inhabitants of the Minneapolis area who claimed no other land;[25] they have no traditions of having immigrated.[26] In 1680, cleric Louis Hennepin, who was probably the first European to see the Minneapolis waterfall the Dakota people call Owámniyomni, renamed it the Falls of St. Anthony of Padua for his patron saint.[27]

Dakota non-combatants interned at a concentration camp at Fort Snelling during the winter of 1862[28][29]

In the space of sixty years, the US seized all of the Dakota land and forced them out of their homeland.[30] Purchasing most of modern-day Minneapolis, Zebulon Pike made the 1805 Treaty of St. Peter with the Dakota.[c] Pike bought a 9-square-mile (23 km2) strip of land—coinciding with the sacred place of Dakota origin[24]—on the Mississippi south of Saint Anthony Falls,[35] with the agreement the US would build a military fort and trading post there and the Dakota would retain their usufructuary rights.[36] In 1819, the US Army built Fort Snelling[37] to direct Native American trade away from British-Canadian traders and to deter war between the Dakota and Ojibwe in northern Minnesota.[38] Under pressure from US officials[39] in a series of treaties, the Dakota ceded their land first to the east and then to the west of the Mississippi, the river that runs through Minneapolis.[40][d] Dakota leaders twice refused to sign the next treaty until they were paid for the previous one.[52] In the decades following these treaty signings, the federal US government rarely honored their terms.[53] At the beginning of the American Civil War, annuity payments owed in June 1862 to the Dakota by treaty were late, causing acute hunger among the Dakota.[54][e] Facing starvation[56] a faction of the Dakota declared war in August and killed settlers.[57] Serving without any prior military experience, US commander Henry Sibley commanded raw recruits,[58] volunteer mounted troops from Minneapolis and Saint Paul with no military experience.[59] The war went on for six weeks in the Minnesota River valley.[60] After a kangaroo court,[61][f] 38 Dakota men were hanged.[60][g] The army force-marched 1,700 non-hostile Dakota men, women, children, and elders 150 miles (240 km) to a concentration camp at Fort Snelling.[28][78] Minneapolitans reportedly threatened more than once to attack the camp.[79] In 1863, the US "abrogated and annulled" all treaties with the Dakota.[80] With Governor Alexander Ramsey calling for their extermination,[81] most Dakota were exiled from Minnesota.[82]

While the Dakota were being expelled, Franklin Steele laid claim to the east bank of Saint Anthony Falls,[83] and John H. Stevens built a home on the west bank.[84] In the Dakota language, the city's name is Bde Óta Othúŋwe ('Many Lakes Town').[h] Residents had divergent ideas on names for their community. Charles Hoag proposed combining the Dakota word for 'water' (mni[i]) with the Greek word for 'city' (polis), yielding Minneapolis. In 1851, after a meeting of the Minnesota Territorial Legislature, leaders of east bank St. Anthony lost their bid to move the capital from Saint Paul, but they eventually won the state university.[90] In 1856, the territorial legislature authorized Minneapolis as a town on the Mississippi's west bank.[5] Minneapolis was incorporated as a city in 1867, and in 1872, it merged with St. Anthony.[91]

Industries developedit
Saint Anthony Falls c. 1850s
Loading flour, Pillsbury, 1939. Photo by John Vachon.

Minneapolis originated around a source of energy: Saint Anthony Falls, the only natural waterfall on the Mississippi.[16] Each of the city's two founding industries—flour and lumber milling—developed in the 19th century nearly concurrently, and each came to prominence for about fifty years.[k] In 1884, the value of Minneapolis flour milling was the world's highest.[96] In 1899, Minneapolis outsold every other lumber market in the world.[97] Through its expanding mill industries, Minneapolis earned the nickname "Mill City".[98] Due to the occupational hazards of milling, six companies manufactured artificial limbs.[99]

Disasters struck in the late 19th century: the Eastman tunnel under the river leaked in 1869; twice, fire destroyed the entire row of sawmills on the east bank;[100] an explosion of flour dust at the Washburn A mill killed eighteen people[101] and demolished about half the city's milling capacity;[102] and in 1893, fire spread from Nicollet Island to Boom Island to northeast Minneapolis, destroyed twenty blocks, and killed two people.[103]

The lumber industry was built around forests in northern Minnesota, largely by lumbermen emigrating from Maine's depleting forests.[104][105] The region's waterways were used to transport logs well after railroads developed; the Mississippi River carried logs to St. Louis until the early 20th century.[106] In 1871, of the thirteen mills sawing lumber in St. Anthony, eight ran on water power, and five ran on steam power.[107] Auxiliary businesses on the river's west bank included woolen mills, iron works, a railroad machine shop, and mills for cotton, paper, sashes, and wood-planing.[108] Minneapolis supplied the materials for farmsteads and settlement of rapidly expanding cities on the prairies that lacked wood.[109] White pine milled in Minneapolis built Miles City, Montana; Bismarck, North Dakota; Sioux Falls, South Dakota; Omaha, Nebraska; and Wichita, Kansas.[110] Growing use of steam power freed lumbermen and their sawmills from dependence on the falls.[111] Lumbering's decline began around the turn of the century,[112] and sawmills in the city including the Weyerhauser mill closed by 1919.[113] After depleting Minnesota's white pine,[114] some lumbermen moved on to Douglas fir in the Pacific Northwest.[115]

Seymour Cray and colleagues began work on the CDC 6600 (pictured) in downtown Minneapolis and completed the project in Chippewa Falls, Wisconsin, in 1963.[116]

In 1877, Cadwallader C. Washburn co-founded Washburn-Crosby,[117] the flour-milling company that became General Mills.[118][l] Washburn and partner John Crosby[119] sent Austrian civil engineer William de la Barre to Hungary where he acquired innovations through industrial espionage.[120] De la Barre calculated and managed the power at the falls and encouraged steam for auxiliary power.[121] C. A. Pillsbury Company across the river hired Washburn-Crosby employees and began using the new methods.[120] Wheat farming developed west across the Great Plains, from Minnesota, to the Dakotas and Montana,[122] and new rail lines connected these farmers to the Minneapolis mills, reciprocally spurring further expansion.[123] The hard red spring wheat grown in Minnesota became valuable, and Minnesota "patent" flour was recognized at the time as the best bread flour in the world.[120] In 1900, fourteen percent of America's grain was milled in Minneapolis[120] and about one third of that was shipped overseas.[124] Overall production peaked at 18.5 million barrels in 1916.[125] Decades of soil exhaustion, stem rust, and changes in freight tariffs combined to quash the city's flour industry.[126] In the 1920s, Washburn-Crosby and Pillsbury developed new milling centers in Buffalo, New York, and Kansas City, Missouri, while maintaining their headquarters in Minneapolis.[127] The falls became a national historic district,[128] and the upper St. Anthony lock and dam was permanently closed to traffic.[129] The city announced that in accordance with a 2020 act of Congress, ownership of 5 acres (2.0 hectares) of federal land around the falls will transfer in 2026 to a Dakota-led nonprofit Owámniyomni Okhódayapi.[130]

Columnist Don Morrison says that after the milling era waned a "modern, major city" emerged.[131] Around 1900, Minneapolis attracted skilled workers[132] who leveraged expertise from the University of Minnesota.[133] In 1923, Munsingwear was the world's largest manufacturer of underwear.[134] Frederick McKinley Jones invented mobile refrigeration in Minneapolis, and with his associate founded Thermo King in 1938.[135] In 1949, Medtronic was founded in a Minneapolis garage.[136] Minneapolis-Honeywell built a south Minneapolis campus where their experience regulating control systems earned them military contracts for the Norden bombsight and the C-1 autopilot.[137] In 1957, Control Data began in downtown Minneapolis,[138] where in the CDC 1604 computer they replaced vacuum tubes with transistors.[139] A highly successful business until disbanded in 1990, Control Data opened a facility in economically depressed north Minneapolis, bringing jobs and good publicity.[138] A University of Minnesota computing group released Gopher in 1991; three years later, the World Wide Web superseded Gopher traffic.[140]

The Mississippi riverfront and Saint Anthony Falls in 1915. At left, Pillsbury, power plants and the Stone Arch Bridge. Today the Minnesota Historical Society's Mill City Museum is in the Washburn "A" Mill, across the river just to the left of the falls. At center-left are Northwestern Consolidated mills. The tall building is Minneapolis City Hall. In the right foreground are Nicollet Island and the Hennepin Avenue Bridge.
Social tensionsedit
Further information: List of incidents of civil unrest in Minneapolis–Saint Paul, 2020–2023 Minneapolis–Saint Paul racial unrest, and Operation Metro Surge
Battle between striking teamsters and police, 1934. The May (pictured) and subsequent July battles killed four men, two on each side.[141]

In many ways, the 20th century in Minneapolis was a difficult time of bigotry and malfeasance, beginning with four decades of corruption.[142] Known initially as a kindly physician, mayor Doc Ames made his brother police chief, ran the city into crime, and tried to leave town in 1902.[143] The Ku Klux Klan was a force in the city from 1921[144] until 1923.[145] The gangster Kid Cann engaged in bribery and intimidation between the 1920s and the 1940s.[146]

During the summer of 1934 and the financial downturn of the Great Depression, the Citizens' Alliance, an association of employers, refused to negotiate with teamsters. The truck drivers union executed strikes in May and July–August.[147] Charles Rumford Walker said that Minneapolis teamsters succeeded in part due to the "military precision of the strike machine".[148] The union victory ultimately led to 1935 and 1938 federal laws protecting workers' rights.[149]

From the end of World War I in 1918 until 1950, antisemitism was commonplace in Minneapolis—Carey McWilliams called the city the antisemitic capital of the US.[150] Starting in 1936, a fascist hate group known as the Silver Shirts held meetings in the city.[151] In the 1940s, mayor Hubert Humphrey worked to rescue the city's reputation[152] and helped the city establish the country's first municipal fair employment practices[153] and a human-relations council that interceded on behalf of minorities.[154] However, the lives of Black people had not been improved.[155] In 1966 and 1967—years of significant turmoil across the US—suppressed anger among the Black population was released in two disturbances on Plymouth Avenue.[156] Historian Iric Nathanson says young Blacks confronted police, arson caused property damage, and "random gunshots" caused minor injuries in what was a "relatively minor incident" in Minneapolis compared to the loss of life and property in similar incidents in Detroit and Newark.[157] A coalition reached a peaceful outcome but again failed to solve Black poverty and unemployment.[158] In the wake of unrest and voter backlash, Charles Stenvig, a law-and-order candidate, became mayor in 1969, and governed for almost a decade.[159][160]

The American Indian Movement's Heart of the Earth Survival School in 1983
General strike march downtown in 2026

Disparate events defined the second half of the 20th century. Between 1958 and 1963, Minneapolis demolished "skid row".[m] Gone were 35 acres (10 ha) with more than 200 buildings, or roughly 40 percent of downtown, including the Gateway District and its significant architecture such as the Metropolitan Building.[162] Opened in 1967, I-35W displaced Black and Mexican neighborhoods[163] in south Minneapolis.[164] In 1968, relocated Native Americans founded the American Indian Movement (AIM)[165] in Minneapolis. Begun as an alternative to public and Bureau of Indian Affairs schools, AIM's Heart of the Earth Survival School taught Native American traditions to children for nearly twenty years.[166] A same-sex Minneapolis couple appealed all the way to the US Supreme Court but their marriage license was denied.[167] They managed to get a license and marry in 1971,[167] forty years before Minnesota legalized same-sex marriage.[168] Immigration helped to curb the city's mid-20th century population decline. But because of a few radicalized persons, the city's large Somali population was targeted with discrimination after 9/11, when its hawalas or banks were closed.[169]

In 2020, 17-year-old Darnella Frazier recorded the murder of George Floyd;[170] Frazier's video contradicted the police department's initial statement.[171] Floyd, a Black man, suffocated when Derek Chauvin, a White Minneapolis police officer, knelt on his neck and back for more than nine minutes. Reporting on the local reaction, The New York Times said that "over three nights, a five-mile stretch of Minneapolis sustained extraordinary damage"[172]—destruction included a police station that demonstrators overran and set on fire.[173] Floyd's murder sparked international rebellions, mass protests,[174] and locally, years of ongoing unrest over racial injustice.[175][176] As of 2024, protest continued daily at the intersection where Floyd died, now known as George Floyd Square, with the slogan "No justice, no street".[176] Protesters continued to ask for twenty-four reforms—many now met; a sticking point was ending qualified immunity for police.[176] Minneapolis gathered ideas for the square and through community engagement construction was scheduled for 2026, with substantial completion by 2027. Applications were being evaluated for a memorial called Peoples' Way.[177]

Operation Metro Surge, a Department of Homeland Security operation involving the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and US Customs and Border Protection began in December 2025, focused on detaining and deporting undocumented immigrants.[178] Initially targeting Minneapolis and Saint Paul,[178] 3,000 agents were deployed in the state.[179] Grassroots activists took trainings to observe and record ICE actions.[180] In January 2026, ICE officers killed Renée Good in Minneapolis;[181] later in the month, Border Patrol agents killed Alex Pretti.[182] Both were US citizens. Tens of thousands engaged in mostly peaceful protests.[183] Operation Metro Surge cost Minneapolis about $700 million for December 2025 through April 2026,[184] including police overtime, and extensive disruption to businesses by federal agents—lost business revenue December through March was estimated at $444 million.[185] Border czar Tom Homan announced the surge's end in February but in March more agents were in the state than before the surge.[179][n] While a preliminary injunction was denied, Minnesota, Minneapolis, and Saint Paul's ongoing lawsuit argues the surge violated the 10th Amendment.[186]

Geographyedit
Main article: Geography of Minneapolis
Further information: Climate of Minnesota, Climate of Minneapolis–Saint Paul, and Geology of Minnesota
The city's largest lake, Bde Maka Ska[187]

The history and economic growth of Minneapolis are linked to water, the city's defining physical characteristic. Long periods of glaciation and interglacial melt carved several riverbeds through what is now Minneapolis.[188] During the last glacial period, around 10,000 years ago, ice buried in these ancient river channels melted, resulting in basins that filled with water to become the lakes of Minneapolis.[189] Meltwater from Lake Agassiz fed the Glacial River Warren, which created a large waterfall that eroded upriver past the confluence of the Mississippi River, where it left a 75-foot (23-meter) drop in the Mississippi.[190] This site is located in what is now downtown Saint Paul. The new waterfall, later called Saint Anthony Falls, in turn, eroded up the Mississippi about eight miles (13 kilometers) to its present location, carving the Mississippi River gorge as it moved upstream. Minnehaha Falls developed during this period via similar processes.[191][190]

Minneapolis is sited above an artesian aquifer[192] and on flat terrain. Its total area is 59 square miles (152.8 square kilometers) of which six percent is covered by water.[193] The city has a 12-mile (19 km) segment of the Mississippi River, four streams, and 17 waterbodies—13 of them lakes,[194] with 24 miles (39 km) of lake shoreline.[195]

A 1959 report by the US Soil Conservation Service listed Minneapolis's elevation above mean sea level as 830 feet (250 meters).[196] The city's lowest elevation of 687 feet (209 m) above sea level is near the confluence of Minnehaha Creek with the Mississippi River.[197] Sources disagree on the exact location and elevation of the city's highest point, which is cited as being between 967 and 985 feet (295 and 300 m) above sea level.[o]

Neighborhoodsedit
Main article: Neighborhoods of Minneapolis
Cyclists on Midtown Greenway in Midtown Phillips, one of the 83 neighborhoods of Minneapolis

Minneapolis has 83 neighborhoods and 70 neighborhood organizations.[200] In some cases, two or more neighborhoods act together under one organization.[201]

Around 1990, the city set up the Neighborhood Revitalization Program (NRP), in which every one of the city's eighty-some neighborhoods participated.[202] Funded for 20 years through 2011, with $400 million tax increment financing[202] ($572 million in 2025),[32] the program caught the eye of UN-Habitat, who considered it an example of best practices. Residents had a direct connection to government in NRP, whereby they proposed ideas appropriate for their area, and NRP reviewed the plans and provided implementation funds.[202][203]

The city's Neighborhood and Community Relations department took NRP's place in 2011[204] and is funded only by city revenue. In 2019, the city released the Neighborhoods 2020 program, which reworked neighborhood funding with an equity-focused lens.[205] This reduced guaranteed funding, and several neighborhood organizations have since struggled with operations or merged with other neighborhoods due to decreased revenue.[206] Base funding for every neighborhood organization increased in the 2024 city budget.[207]

In 2018, the Minneapolis City Council approved the Minneapolis 2040 Comprehensive Plan, which resulted in a citywide end to single-family zoning.[208] Slate reported that Minneapolis was the first major city in the US to make citywide such a revision in housing possibilities.[209] At the time, 70 percent of residential land was zoned for detached, single-family homes,[210] though many of those areas had "nonconforming" buildings with more housing units.[211] City leaders sought to increase the supply of housing to create more affordable housing and to decrease the effects single-family zoning had caused on racial disparities and segregation.[212] The Brookings Institution called it "a relatively rare example of success for the YIMBY agenda".[213] From 2022 until 2024,[214][215] the Minnesota Supreme Court, the US District Court, and the Minnesota Court of Appeals arrived at competing opinions, first shutting down the plan, and then securing its survival. Ultimately in 2024, the state legislature passed a bill approving the city's 2040 plan.[216] In the years following the 2040 Plan, rent increases slowed in Minneapolis relative to comparison cities; the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis pointed out the difficulty of disentangling potential effects of the plan from other market factors.[217]

Climateedit
Further information: Climate of Minneapolis–Saint Paul

Minneapolis has a hot-summer humid continental climate (Dfa in the Köppen climate classification)[218] that is typical of southern parts of the Upper Midwest. It is in USDA plant hardiness zone 5a.[219][220][221] The Minneapolis area experiences a full range of precipitation and related weather events, including snow, sleet, ice, rain, thunderstorms, and fog. The highest recorded temperature is 108 °F (42 °C) in July 1936. The lowest was −41 °F (−41 °C) in January 1888.[222]

The snowiest winter on record was 1983–1984, when 98.6 in (250 cm) of snow fell.[223] The least-snowy winter was 1930–1931, when 14.2 inches (36 cm) fell.[223] According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the annual average for sunshine duration is 58 percent.[224]
