The Minneapolis area was originally occupied by Dakota bands, particularly the Mdewakanton, until European Americans moved westward.[230] In the 1840s,[231] new settlers arrived from Maine, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts, while French-Canadians came around the same time.[232][233] Farmers from Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, and Pennsylvania followed in a secondary migration. Settlers from New England had an outsized influence on civic life.[234]

Mexican migrant workers began coming to Minnesota as early as 1860, although few stayed year-round.[235] Latinos eventually settled in several neighborhoods in Minneapolis, including Phillips, Whittier, Longfellow and Northeast.[236] Before the turn of the 21st century, Latinos were the state's largest and fastest-growing immigrant group.[235][237]

Immigrants from Sweden, Norway, and Denmark found common ground with the Republican and Protestant belief systems of the New England migrants who preceded them.[238][239] Irish, Scots, and English immigrants arrived after the Civil War;[240] Germans[241] and Jews from Central and Eastern Europe, as well as Russia, followed.[242] Minneapolis welcomed Italians and Greeks in the 1890s and 1900s,[243][244] and Slovak and Czech immigrants settled in the Bohemian Flats area on the west bank of the Mississippi River. Ukrainians arrived after 1900,[245] and Central European migrants made their homes in the Northeast neighborhood.[246]

Chinese began immigration in the 1870s and Chinese businesses centered on the Gateway District and Glenwood Avenue.[247] Westminster Presbyterian Church gave language classes and support for Chinese Americans in Minneapolis, many of whom had fled discrimination in western states.[248] Japanese Americans, many relocated from San Francisco, worked at Camp Savage, a secret military Japanese-language school that trained interpreters and translators.[249] Following World War II, some Japanese and Japanese Americans remained in Minneapolis, and by 1970, they numbered nearly 2,000, forming part of the state's largest Asian American community.[250] In the 1950s, the US government relocated Native Americans to cities like Minneapolis, attempting to dismantle Indian reservations.[251] Around 1970, Koreans arrived,[252] and the first Filipinos came to attend the University of Minnesota.[253] Vietnamese, Hmong (some from Thailand), Lao, and Cambodians settled mainly in Saint Paul around 1975, but some built organizations in Minneapolis.[254][255] In 1992, 160 Tibetan immigrants came to Minnesota, and many settled in the city's Whittier neighborhood.[256] Burmese immigrants arrived in the early 2000s, with some moving to Greater Minnesota.[257] The population of people from India in Minneapolis increased by 1,000 between 2000 and 2010, making it the largest concentration of Indians living in the state.[258]

The population of Minneapolis grew until 1950 when the census peaked at 521,718—the only time it has exceeded a half million. The population then declined for decades; after World War II, people moved to the suburbs and generally out of the Midwest.[259]

By 1930, Minneapolis had one of the nation's highest literacy rates among Black residents.[260][261][262] However, discrimination prevented them from obtaining higher-paying jobs.[263] In 1935, Cecil Newman and the Minneapolis Spokesman led a year-long consumer boycott of four area breweries that refused to hire Blacks.[264] Employment improved during World War II, but housing discrimination persisted.[265] Between 1950 and 1970, the Black population in Minneapolis increased by 436 percent.[264] After the Rust Belt economy declined in the 1980s, Black migrants were attracted to Minneapolis for its job opportunities, good schools, and safe neighborhoods.[266] In the 1990s, immigrants from the Horn of Africa began to arrive,[267] from Eritrea, Ethiopia, and particularly Somalia.[268] Immigration from Somalia slowed significantly following a 2017 national executive order.[269] As of 2022, about 3,000 Ethiopians and 20,000 Somalis reside in Minneapolis.[270]

The Williams Institute reported that the Twin Cities had an estimated 4.2-percent LGBT adult population in 2020.[271] In 2023, the Human Rights Campaign gave Minneapolis 94 points out of 100 on the Municipal Equality Index of support for the LGBTQ+ population.[272] Twin Cities Pride is held every June.[273]

Census and estimatesedit

Minneapolis is the most populous city in Minnesota and the 46th-most populous city in the United States by population as of 2024.[274][275] According to the 2020 US Census, Minneapolis had a population of 429,954.[276] Of this population, 44,513 (10.4 percent) identified as Hispanic or Latinos.[277] Of those not Hispanic or Latino, 249,581 persons (58.0 percent) were White alone (62.7 percent White alone or in combination), 81,088 (18.9 percent) were Black or African American alone (21.3 percent Black alone or in combination), 24,929 (5.8 percent) were Asian alone, 7,433 (1.2 percent) were American Indian and Alaska Native alone, 25,387 (0.6 percent) some other race alone, and 34,463 (5.2 percent) were multiracial.[276]

The most common ancestries in Minneapolis according to the 2021 American Community Survey (ACS) were German (22.9 percent), Irish (10.8 percent), Norwegian (8.9 percent), Sub-Saharan African (6.7 percent), and Swedish (6.1 percent).[278] Among those five years and older, 81.2 percent spoke only English at home, while 7.1 percent spoke Spanish and 11.7 percent spoke other languages, including large numbers of Somali and Hmong speakers.[278] About 13.7 percent of the population was born abroad, with 53.2 percent of them being naturalized US citizens. Most immigrants arrived from Africa (40.6 percent), Latin America (25.2 percent), and Asia (24.6 percent), with 34.6 percent of all foreign-born residents having arrived in 2010 or earlier.[278]

The ACS reported that the 2021 median household income in Minneapolis was $69,397 ($82,453 in 2025), similar to the US household median income of $70,784 in 2021.[279][32] The median household income was $97,670 for families, $123,693 for married couples, and $54,083 for non-family households.[280][281] In 2023, the median Minneapolis rent was $1,529, compared to the national median of $1,723.[282] Over 92 percent of housing units in Minneapolis were occupied.[283] Housing units in the city built in 1939 or earlier comprised 43.7 percent.[283] Almost 17 percent of residents lived in poverty in 2023, compared to the US average of 11.1 percent.[284] As of 2022, 90.8 percent of residents age 25 years or older had earned a high school degree compared to 89.1 percent nationally, and 53.5 percent had a bachelor's degree or higher compared to the 34.3 percent US national average.[284] US veterans made up 2.8 percent of the population compared to the national average of 5 percent in 2023.[284]

In Minneapolis in 2020, Blacks owned homes at a rate one-third that of White families.[285] Statewide by 2022, the gap between White and Black home ownership declined from 51.5 percent to 48 percent.[286] Statewide, alongside this small improvement was a sharp increase in the Black-to-White comparative number of deaths of despair (e.g., alcohol, drugs, and suicide).[286] The Minneapolis income gap in 2018 was one of the largest in the country, with Black families earning about 44 percent of what White families earned annually.[285] Statewide in 2022 using inflation-adjusted dollars, the median income for a Black family was $34,377 less than a White family's median income, an improvement of $7,000 since 2019.[286]

Structural racismedit

Before 1910,[155] when a developer wrote the first restrictive covenant based on race and ethnicity into a Minneapolis deed,[291] the city was relatively unsegregated with a Black population of less than one percent.[292] Realtors adopted the practice, thousands of times preventing non-Whites from owning or leasing properties;[293] this practice continued for four decades until the city became more and more racially divided.[294] Though such language was prohibited by state law in 1953 and by the federal Fair Housing Act of 1968,[295] restrictive covenants against minorities remained in many Minneapolis deeds as of the 2020s. In 2021, the city gave residents a means to discharge them.[296]

Minneapolis has a history of structural racism[297] and has racial disparities in nearly every aspect of society.[298] As White settlers displaced the Indigenous population during the 19th century, they claimed the city's land,[299] and Kirsten Delegard of Mapping Prejudice explains that today's disparities evolved from control of the land.[155] Discrimination increased when flour milling moved to the East Coast and the economy declined.[300]

The foundation laid by racial covenants on residential segregation, property value, homeownership, wealth, housing security, access to green spaces, and health equity shapes the lives of people in the 21st century.[301] The city wrote in a decennial plan that racially discriminatory federal housing policies starting in the 1930s "prevented access to mortgages in areas with Jews, African-Americans and other minorities" and "left a lasting effect on the physical characteristics of the city and the financial well-being of its residents".[302]

Discussing a Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis report on how systemic racism compromises education in Minnesota,[303] Professor Keith Mayes says, "So the housing disparities created the educational disparities that we still live with today."[304] Professor Samuel Myers Jr. says of redlining, "Policing policies evolved that substituted explicit racial profiling with scientific management of racially disparate arrests. ... racially discriminatory policies became institutionalized and 'baked in' to the fabric of Minnesota life."[305][r] Government efforts to address these disparities included zoning changes passed in the 2040 plan,[307] and declaring racism a public health emergency in 2020.[308]

Religionedit
Further information: Religion in Minnesota
Christ Church Lutheran is one of the city's four National Historic Landmarks.[309]

Twin Cities residents are 59 percent Christian according to a Pew Research Center religious survey in 2023-24. The largest groups are Mainline Protestant (21%), Catholic (18%) and Evangelical Protestant (16%).[310] Settlers who arrived in Minneapolis from New England were for the most part Protestants, Quakers, and Universalists.[311] The oldest continuously used church, Our Lady of Lourdes Catholic Church, was built in 1856 by Universalists and soon afterward was acquired by a French Catholic congregation.[312] St. Mary's Orthodox Cathedral was founded in 1887;[313] it opened a missionary school and in 1905 created a Russian Orthodox seminary.[314] Edwin Hawley Hewitt designed St. Mark's Episcopal Cathedral and Hennepin Avenue United Methodist Church, both of which are located south of downtown.[315] The nearby Basilica of Saint Mary, the first basilica in the US and co-cathedral of the Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis, was named by Pope Pius XI in 1926.[311] The Billy Graham Evangelistic Association was headquartered in Minneapolis from the 1950s until 2001.[316] Christ Church Lutheran in the Longfellow neighborhood was the final work in the career of Eliel Saarinen, and it has an education building designed by his son Eero.[317]

Aligning with a national trend, the metro area's next largest group after Christians is the 34-percent non-religious population.[310] At the same time, more than 50 denominations and religions are present in Minneapolis, representing most of the world's religions.[311] Temple Israel was built in 1928 by the city's first Jewish congregation, Shaarai Tov, which formed in 1878.[242] By 1959, a Temple of Islam was located in north Minneapolis.[318] In 1971, a reported 150 persons attended classes at a Hindu temple near the University of Minnesota.[318] In 1972, the Twin Cities' first Shi'a Muslim family resettled from Uganda.[319] Somalis who live in Minneapolis are primarily Sunni Muslim.[320] In 2022, Minneapolis amended its noise ordinance to allow broadcasting the Muslim call to prayer five times per day.[321] The city has about seven Buddhist centers and meditation centers.[322]

Early in the city's history, millers were required to pay for wheat with cash during the growing season and then to store the wheat until it was needed for flour.[325] The Minneapolis Grain Exchange was founded in 1881; located near the riverfront, it is the only exchange as of 2023 for hard red spring wheat futures.[326]

Along with cash requirements for the milling industry, the large amounts of capital that lumbering had accumulated stimulated the local banking industry and made Minneapolis a major financial center.[327] The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis serves Minnesota, Montana, North and South Dakota, and parts of Wisconsin and Michigan; it has the smallest population of the twelve districts in the Federal Reserve System, and it has one branch in Helena, Montana.[328]

Minneapolis area employment is primarily in trade, transportation, utilities, education, health services, and professional and business services. Smaller numbers of residents are employed in government, manufacturing, leisure and hospitality, and financial activities.[329]

In 2024, the Twin Cities metropolitan area had the eighth-highest concentration of major corporate headquarters in the US.[330] Five Fortune 500 corporations were headquartered within the city limits of Minneapolis:[324] Target Corporation, U.S. Bancorp, Xcel Energy, Ameriprise Financial, and Thrivent.[324] The metro area's gross domestic product was $350.7 billion in 2023[12] ($371 billion in 2025).[32]

Arts and cultureedit
Main article: Arts in Minneapolis
Visual artsedit
The Minneapolis Institute of Art admission is free except for special exhibitions.[331]

During the Gilded Age, the Walker Art Center began as a private art collection in the home of lumberman T. B. Walker, who extended free admission to the public.[332] Around 1940, the center's focus shifted to modern and contemporary art.[333] In partnership with the Minneapolis Park and Recreation Board, the Walker operates the adjacent Minneapolis Sculpture Garden, which has about forty sculptures on view year-round.[334]

The Minneapolis Institute of Art (Mia) is located in south-central Minneapolis on the 10-acre (4 ha) former homestead of the Morrison family.[335] McKim, Mead & White designed a vast complex meeting the ambitions of the founders for a cultural center with spaces for sculpture, an art school, and orchestra. One-seventh of their design was built and opened in 1915. Additions by other firms from 1928 to 2006 achieved much of the original scheme.[336] Today the collection of more than 90,000 artworks spans six continents and about 5,000 years.[337]

Frank Gehry designed Weisman Art Museum, which opened in 1993, for the University of Minnesota.[338] A 2011 addition by Gehry doubled the size of the galleries.[339] The Museum of Russian Art opened in a restored church in 2005, and it hosts a collection of 20th-century Russian art and special events.[340] The Northeast Minneapolis Arts District hosts 400 independent artists and a center at the Northrup-King building, and it presents the Art-A-Whirl open studio tour every May.[341][342]

Theater and performing artsedit
Further information: List of theaters in Minnesota
The Guthrie Theater originated as an alternative to Broadway.[343]

Minneapolis has hosted theatrical performances since the end of the American Civil War.[344] Early theaters included Pence Opera House, the Academy of Music, Grand Opera House, Lyceum, and later the Metropolitan Opera House, which opened in 1894.[345] Fifteen of the fifty-five Twin Cities theater companies counted in 2015 by Peg Guilfoyle had a physical site in Minneapolis. About half the remainder performed in variable spaces throughout the metropolitan area.[346]

In his social history of American regional theater, Joseph Zeigler calls the Guthrie Theater the "granddaddy" of regional theater.[347] Tyrone Guthrie founded the Guthrie in 1963 with an inventive thrust stage—a collaboration by Guthrie, designer Tanya Moiseiwitsch, and architect Ralph Rapson[348]—jutting into the seats and surrounded by the audience on three sides.[349] French architect Jean Nouvel designed a new Guthrie that opened in 2006 overlooking the Mississippi River.[349] The design team reproduced the thrust stage with some alterations, and they added a proscenium stage and an experimental stage.[349]

Minneapolis purchased and renovated the Orpheum, Shubert (now the Cowles Center for Dance and the Performing Arts), State, and Pantages theaters, vaudeville and film houses on Hennepin Avenue that are now used for concerts, plays,[350] and performing arts.[351] Every August, the Minnesota Fringe Festival hosts performances in venues across town.[352] The May Day Parade is held in south Minneapolis each May.[353][354]

Musicedit
Further information: Music of Minnesota
Prince studied at the Minnesota Dance Theatre[355] through the Minneapolis Public Schools.[356]

Minnesota Orchestra plays classical and popular music at Orchestra Hall under music director Thomas Søndergård.[357] The orchestra won a 2014 Grammy for their recording of Sibelius's first and fourth symphonies[358] and a 2004 Grammy for composer Dominick Argento with their recording of Casa Guidi.[359] Minneapolis's opera companies include Minnesota Opera,[360][s] the Gilbert & Sullivan Very Light Opera Company,[361] and Really Spicy Opera.[362]

Singer and multi-instrumentalist Prince was a child prodigy[363] who was born in Minneapolis and lived in the area for most of his life.[364] In an era of music scenes,[365] 1980s Minneapolis was a hotbed for American underground rock alongside R&B, funk, and soul[366] thanks to the nightclub First Avenue and musicians like Hüsker Dü, The Replacements, and Prince.[367] The city hosts several other concert venues including the Cedar and the Dakota.[368] The Armory, the Skyway Theatre,[369] and the Uptown Theater have national management.[370]

Historical museumsedit
Black Lives Matter mural (2020) organized by the Minnesota African American Heritage Museum and Gallery[371]

Exhibits at Mill City Museum feature the city's history of flour milling.[372] The Bakken, formerly known as the Bakken Library and Museum of Electricity in Life,[373] shifted focus in 2016 from electricity and magnetism to invention and innovation, and in 2020 opened a new entrance on Bde Maka Ska.[374] Hennepin History Museum is housed in a former mansion.[375] Built of elaborate woodwork in 1875 and maintained today as a historic site, the little Minnehaha Depot was a stop on one of the first railroads built out of Minneapolis.[376]

The American Swedish Institute occupies a former mansion on Park Avenue.[377] The American Indian Cultural Corridor, about eight blocks on Franklin Avenue, houses All My Relatives Gallery.[378] In 2013, the Somali Museum of Minnesota opened on Lake Street.[379] The Minnesota African American Heritage Museum and Gallery was founded in 2018.[380]

Libraries and literary artsedit
Main article: Hennepin County Library

In 2008, the Minneapolis Public Library merged with the Hennepin County Library. Fifteen of the system's forty-one branches serve Minneapolis.[381] The downtown Central Library, designed by César Pelli, opened in 2006.[382] Seven special collections hold resources for researchers.[383]

The nonprofit literary presses Coffee House Press, Graywolf Press, and Milkweed Editions are based in Minneapolis.[384] The University of Minnesota Press publishes books, journals, and the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory.[385] The Open Book facility houses The Loft Literary Center, Milkweed, and the Minnesota Center for Book Arts.[386] Other Minneapolis publishers are 1517 Media,[387] Button Poetry,[388] and Lerner Publishing Group.[389]

Cuisineedit
Further information: Cuisine of the Midwestern United States § Minneapolis and Saint Paul

After the flight to the suburbs began in the 1950s, streetcar service ended citywide.[390] One of the largest urban food deserts in the US developed on the north side of Minneapolis, where as of mid-2017, 70,000 people had access to only two grocery stores.[391] When Aldi closed in 2023, the area again became a food desert with two full-service grocers.[392] The nonprofit Appetite for Change sought to improve the diet of residents, competing against an influx of fast-food stores,[393] and by 2017 it administered ten gardens, sold produce in the mid-year months at West Broadway Farmers Market, supplied its restaurants, and gave away boxes of fresh produce.[394] Appetite for Change closed its Minneapolis restaurant in 2023, opened a food truck, and received a grant from the Minnesota legislature to create a long-term home.[395] West Broadway is one of twenty farmers markets and mini-markets operating in the city, and among them, four are open during winter.[396]

Minneapolis-based individuals who have won the food industry James Beard Foundation Award include chef Gavin Kaysen,[397] writer Dara Moskowitz Grumdahl,[398] television personality Andrew Zimmern,[399] and chef Sean Sherman,[400] whose restaurant Owamni received James Beard's 2022 best new restaurant award.[401] James Beard's best new restaurant of 2025 was Bûcheron.[402]

Conceived in Minneapolis as a malted milkshake in candy form, the Milky Way bar of nougat, caramel, and chocolate was made in the North Loop neighborhood during the 1920s.[403] Both purported originators of the Jucy Lucy burger—the 5-8 Club and Matt's Bar—have served it since the 1950s.[404] East African cuisine arrived in Minneapolis with the wave of migrants from Somalia that started in the 1990s.[405] The Herbivorous Butcher, described by CBS News as the "first vegan 'butcher' shop in the United States", opened in 2016.[406]

Sportsedit
Main articles: Sports in Minneapolis–Saint Paul and Sports in Minnesota
Target Center
Target Field
U.S. Bank Stadium

Minneapolis has four professional sports teams. The American football team Minnesota Vikings and the baseball team Minnesota Twins have played in the state since 1961. The Vikings were a National Football League expansion team, and the Twins were formed when the Washington Senators relocated to Minnesota.[407] The Twins won the World Series in 1987 and 1991, and have played at Target Field since 2010.[408] The Vikings played in the Super Bowl following the 1969, 1973, 1974, and 1976 seasons, losing all four games.[409]

The basketball team Minnesota Timberwolves returned National Basketball Association (NBA) basketball to Minneapolis in 1989, and were followed by Minnesota Lynx in 1999. Both basketball teams play in the Target Center.[410] The Lynx were the most-successful Minnesota professional sports team and a dominant force in the Women's National Basketball Association (WNBA), losing the 2024 finals[411] and winning four WNBA championships from 2011 to 2017.[412]

Minnesota Frost, the champion Professional Women's Hockey League team in 2024 and 2025,[413] and the Minnesota Wild, a National Hockey League team, play at the Grand Casino Arena,[414] and the Major League Soccer soccer team Minnesota United FC play at Allianz Field. Both venues are located in Saint Paul.[415]

In addition to professional sports teams, Minneapolis hosts a majority of the Minnesota Golden Gophers' college sports teams of the University of Minnesota. As of 2026, the Minnesota Golden Gophers Spirit Squads have won 30 combined cheer and dance national championships.[416] The Gophers football team plays at Huntington Bank Stadium and has won seven national championships.[417] The Gophers women's ice hockey team is a six-time NCAA champion.[418] The Gophers men's ice hockey team plays at 3M Arena at Mariucci, and won five NCAA championships.[419] Both the Golden Gophers men's basketball and women's basketball teams play at Williams Arena.[420]

The 1,700,000-square-foot (160,000 m2) U.S. Bank Stadium was built for the Vikings at a cost of $1.122 billion ($1.57 billion in 2025);[32] of this, the state of Minnesota provided $348 million ($488 million in 2025),[32] and the city of Minneapolis spent $150 million ($210 million in 2025).[32] The stadium, which MPR News called "Minnesota's biggest-ever public works project", opened in 2016 with 66,000 seats, which was expanded to 70,000 for the 2018 Super Bowl.[421] U.S. Bank Stadium also hosts indoor running and rollerblading nights.[422] Minneapolis has two municipal golf courses[423] and one private course.[424] Each January, the U.S. Pond Hockey Championships are held on Lake Nokomis.[425] The final weekend of the 2024 championships was canceled due to above average temperatures.[426] A Boston Marathon qualifier,[427] the Twin Cities Marathon moved from early- to mid-October because of rising temperatures.[428]

Parks and recreationedit
Main article: Minneapolis Park and Recreation Board
Minnehaha Falls in the summer

Landscape architect Horace Cleveland's masterpiece is the Minneapolis park system.[429] In the 1880s, he preserved geographical landmarks and linked them with boulevards and parkways.[430] In their introduction to a modern reprint of Cleveland's treatise on landscape architecture, professors Daniel Nadenicek and Lance Neckar add that "Cleveland was successful in Minneapolis in great measure because he operated with kindred spirits" like William Watts Folwell and Charles M. Loring.[431] In his book The American City: What Works, What Doesn't, Alexander Garvin wrote Minneapolis built "the best-located, best-financed, best-designed, and best-maintained public open space in America".[432]

Cleveland lobbied for a park on the riverfront to include the city's other waterfall.[433] In 1889, George A. Brackett arranged financing, and his associate Henry Brown paid the state to cover the condemnation of surrounding land.[434] Minnehaha Park, containing the 53-foot (16 m) waterfall Minnehaha Falls, is one of Minnesota's first state parks.[435] The falls became what historian Mary Lethert Wingerd calls a "civic emblem" that appears on products and in placenames.[436]

The city's parks are governed and operated by the independent Minneapolis Park and Recreation Board park district.[437] Beyond its network of 185 neighborhood parks,[438] the park board owns the city's street trees.[439][t] The board owns nearly all land that borders the city's waterfronts—thus the public owns the city's lakeshore property.[441] The park board owns land outside the city limits including its largest park, Theodore Wirth Park—sitting west of downtown Minneapolis and partly in Golden Valley—which incorporates the Eloise Butler Wildflower Garden and Bird Sanctuary.[442]

Canoeing on the Mississippi

As of 2020, approximately 15 percent of land in Minneapolis is parks, in accordance with the national median, and 98 percent of residents live within one-half mile (0.8 km) of a park.[443] The city's Chain of Lakes extends through five lakes in southwest Minneapolis.[444] The chain is connected by bicycle, running, and walking paths and is used for swimming, fishing, picnics, boating, ice skating, and other activities. A parkway for cars, a bikeway for riders, and a walkway for pedestrians[445] run parallel along the 51-mile (82 km) route of the Grand Rounds National Scenic Byway.[446]

Parks are interlinked in many places, and the Mississippi National River and Recreation Area connects regional parks and visitor centers.[447] Among walks and hikes running along the Mississippi River, the five-mile (8 km), hiking-only Winchell Trail offers views of and access to the Mississippi Gorge and a rustic hiking experience.[448] The Minneapolis Aquatennial, a civic celebration of the "City of Lakes", is held each July.[449]

Minneapolis's climate provides opportunities for winter activities such as ice fishing, snowshoeing, ice skating, cross-country skiing, and sledding at many parks and lakes.[450] As of 2024, the park board maintained 43 outdoor ice rinks at 20 sites in winter.[451]

Governmentedit
Main articles: Minneapolis City Council, Government of Minneapolis, and Minneapolis Police Department
Further information: List of mayors of Minneapolis and Timeline of race relations and policing in Minneapolis–Saint Paul
Built between 1889 and 1906, Minneapolis City Hall, seen from The People's Plaza, is on the National Register of Historic Places.[452]

Through its municipal branch, the Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party (DFL), affiliated with the national Democratic Party, is the dominant political force in Minneapolis.[453] The city has not elected a Republican mayor since 1975.[454] At the federal level, Minneapolis is in Minnesota's 5th congressional district, which has been represented by Democrat Ilhan Omar since 2018. Both of Minnesota's US senators, Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith, are Democrats who were elected or appointed while residing in Minneapolis.[455][456] Jacob Frey, a former city council member,[457] was elected as the mayor of Minneapolis in 2017 and re-elected in 2021 and 2025.[458] The city conducts its municipal elections using instant-runoff voting, which was first implemented ahead of the 2009 elections.[459]

The Minneapolis City Council has 13 members who represent the city's 13 wards.[460] In 2021, a ballot question shifted more weight from the city council to the mayor; proponents had tried to achieve this change since the early 20th century.[461] The mayor and city council now share responsibility for the city's finances.[462] The city's primary source of funding is property tax.[463] A sales tax of 9.03 percent[464] on purchases made within the city is a combination of the city sales tax of 0.50 percent, along with county, state, and special district taxes.[465][466] The Park and Recreation Board is an independent city department with nine elected commissioners who levy their own taxes, subject to city charter limits.[437] The Board of Estimation and Taxation, which oversees city levies, is also an independent department.[467]

The mayoral reform ballot measure led to four direct reports to the mayor—two officers, the city attorney, and the chief of staff—and the creation of two new offices.[468] The Office of Public Service is led by the city operations officer. The Minneapolis departments of civil rights and public works report to the office which oversees communications and engagement; development, health, and livability; and internal operations. The Office of Community Safety has a single commissioner responsible for overseeing the police and fire departments, 911 dispatch, emergency management, and violence prevention;[469] within this office, four emergency response units serve the city: Behavioral Crisis Response (BCR), fire, emergency medical services, and police.[470] Canopy Mental Health & Consulting, also known as Canopy Roots, operates BCR free of charge[470] to respond to crises and some 911 calls that do not require police.[471]

Police guard the third precinct the day before it was burned down during the George Floyd protests.

After the murder of George Floyd in 2020, about 166 police officers left of their own accord either to retirement or to temporary leave—many with PTSD[472]—and a crime wave resulted in more than 500 shootings.[473] A Reuters investigation found that killings surged when a "hands-off" attitude resulted in fewer officer-initiated encounters.[474] After Floyd's murder, chiefs reprimanded a dozen officers for misconduct,[475] and as of early 2024, the city had paid out $50 million for police conduct claims.[476] In 2024 came approval of an independent monitor of a court-enforceable consent decree, an agreement negotiated with the Minnesota Department of Human Rights and the United States Department of Justice to compel reformed policing practices.[477] In May 2025, the Trump administration moved to dismiss the consent decree.[478]

Violent crime rose three percent across Minneapolis in July 2022 compared with 2021,[479] and in 2020, it rose 21 percent compared to the average of the previous five years.[480] Violent crime was down for 2022 in every category except assaults. Carjackings, gunshots fired, gunshot wounds, and robberies decreased, and homicides were down 20 percent compared to the previous year.[481]

In 2015, the city council passed a resolution making fossil fuel divestment city policy,[482] joining 17 cities worldwide in the Carbon Neutral Cities Alliance. Minneapolis's climate plan calls for an 80-percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.[483] In 2021, the city council voted unanimously to abolish its required minimum number of parking spaces for new construction.[484] Minneapolis has a separation ordinance that directs local law-enforcement officers not to "take any law enforcement action" for the sole purpose of finding undocumented immigrants, nor to ask an individual about their immigration status.[485]

Educationedit
Primary and secondaryedit

In 1834, volunteer missionaries Gideon and Samuel Pond[486] sought permission for their work from the US Indian agency at Fort Snelling.[487] They taught new farming techniques and their Christian religion to Chief Cloud Man and his Dakota community on the east shore of Bde Maka Ska.[311] That year, J. D. Stevens and the Ponds built an Indian mission near Lake Harriet, which was the first educational institution in the Minneapolis area.[311] In the treaty of 1837, the US promised payment to the Dakota, but instead gave the monies to the missionaries earmarked for education, and in protest, fewer than ten Dakota students attended.[488] After more settlers moved to the area, ten school buildings served nearly 4,000 students by 1874. The district had more than one hundred schools when enrollment peaked at 90,000 students in 1933.[489]

A dual language science outreach at Emerson, one of nine[490] magnet elementary schools

Minneapolis Public Schools has room for 45,000 students and enrolled about 28,500 K–12 students as of 2024,[491] in more than fifty schools, divided between community and magnet.[492] Poor financial oversight of the district resulted in a $37.9 million deficit—and thus staff layoffs—for the 2025–2026 school year.[493] As of 2023, enrollment was declining about 1.5 percent per year, and approximately 60 percent of school age children attended district schools.[494] The city offered two reasons for the decline: a dwindling number of children lived in the city since 2020 and, accounting for one-fifth of the decline, the climbing popularity of charter schools and open enrollment.[495] Many students enrolled in alternatives such as charter schools, of which the city had 28 as of 2024.[496] By state law, charter schools are open to all students and are tuition-free.[497] In 2022, about 1200 at-risk students attended district alternative schools that offered them better outcomes than traditional schools.[498] For the 2022–2023 school year, 368 students were homeschooled in Minneapolis.[499]

School district demographics were 41 percent White students, 35 percent Black, 14 percent Hispanic, and 5 percent each were Asian and Native American.[500] English-language learners were about 17 percent[500] in a district that spoke 100 languages at home.[501] About 15 percent were special education students.[500] As of fall 2023, every public school student in the state receives one free breakfast and one free lunch each school day.[502] In 2025, the district's overall graduation rate was 73 percent, a percent less than the previous year.[503]

Colleges and universitiesedit
See also: Minnesota State Colleges and Universities system
University of Minnesota teaching art museum, teaching hospital, and student union (left to right)

Headquartered in Minneapolis, the University of Minnesota Twin Cities campus enrolled more than 45,000 students in 2025–2026.[504] College rankings in 2025–2026 place the school in the range of 51st[505] to 210th for academics worldwide.[506][507] QS found a decline in rank over a decade.[507] Shanghai found excellence in communication, psychology, and library and information science.[505] Among the 2,250 schools U.S. News & World Report compared in its 2025-2026 best global universities rankings, the University of Minnesota ranked 72nd.[504] The school has unusual autonomy that has existed in Minnesota since 1858, when the state constitution included the provision that regents are in control, independent of city government.[508] Founded in 1851[507] and closed in its first decade for lack of funding, the University of Minnesota was revived under the Morrill Act of 1862 using land taken from the Dakota people.[509][u]

Augsburg University, Minneapolis College of Art and Design, and North Central University are private four-year colleges; the first two offer master's programs.[512] The public two-year Minneapolis Community and Technical College[513] and the private Dunwoody College of Technology[514] provide career training and associate degrees, and the latter offers a bachelor's program. Saint Mary's University of Minnesota has a Twin Cities campus for its graduate and professional programs.[515] Opening a new Minneapolis site in 2024, Red Lake Nation College is an accredited federally recognized tribal college site that teaches Ojibwe culture and awards associate degrees.[516] The large, principally online universities Capella University[517] and Walden University[518] are both headquartered in the city. The public four-year Metropolitan State University[519] and the private four-year University of St. Thomas[520] are post-secondary institutions based elsewhere that have campuses in Minneapolis. The city has more than twenty-five licensed career schools.[521]

Mediaedit
Main article: Media in Minneapolis–Saint Paul

As of March 2024, Minnesota Newspaper Association members who publish in Minneapolis include Insight News, Finance & Commerce, Longfellow Nokomis Messenger, Minneapolis/St. Paul Business Journal, Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder, Minnesota Women's Press, North News, Northeaster, Southwest Connector, Star Tribune, and St. Paul – Midway Como Frogtown Monitor.[522] La Prensa de Minnesota,[523] Vida y Sabor,[524] and The American Jewish World[525] are published in the city.[526] Other papers are Southwest Voices,[527] Streets.mn,[528] Bring Me The News,[529] Racket,[530] MinnPost,[531] and Minnesota Daily.[532]

Media Tales called Minnesota a "plentiful" source of national trade magazines; companies in Minneapolis publish Foodservice News and Franchise Times.[533] Some other magazines published in the city are American Craft;[534] business publications Enterprise Minnesota[535] and Twin Cities Business;[536] the literary journal Rain Taxi;[537] university student publications Great River Review,[538] Minnesota Journal of International Law,[539] and Minnesota Law Review;[540] and professional magazines Architecture Minnesota,[541] Bench & Bar,[542] and Minnesota Medicine.[543]

In 2023, Nielsen found the Minneapolis–Saint Paul area to be the 15th-largest designated market area which is down from 14th in 2022.[544] Of the 89 FM and 57 AM stations that can be heard in the city, 17 FM stations and 11 AM stations are licensed in Minneapolis.[545] The Twin Cities have 1,742,530 TV homes.[546] TV Guide lists 151 TV channels for Minneapolis.[547]

Infrastructureedit
Transportationedit
Main articles: Transportation in Minnesota, Metro (Minnesota), and Trails in Minneapolis
A Green Line train traveling from the Stadium Village station
Metro Transit trip agents on the Blue Line in 2024

For all trips by all members of a household in 2019, Metropolitan Council data showed that the most common means of transportation was driving alone (40 percent), the least common was bicycling (3 percent), and others were carpooling (28 percent), walking (16 percent), and public transit (13 percent). The city's goal is that by 2030, 60 percent of trips are taken without a car, or 35 percent by walking and biking and 25 percent by transit. The city aims to reduce vehicle miles traveled by 1.8 percent per year.[548]

A division of the Metropolitan Council, Metro Transit operates public transportation in the Minneapolis–Saint Paul metropolitan area.[549] As of 2026, the system has two light rail lines and eight bus rapid transit (BRT) lines.[550][551] A fleet of 736 buses serves 10,745 bus stops.[552] As of 2021, riders of Metro Transit system-wide were 55 percent persons of color.[552] The system provided nearly 45 million rides in 2023, a sixteen-percent increase over the previous year.[553] In 2023, bus service had returned to 90 percent of its ridership before the COVID-19 pandemic.[553]

The Metro Blue Line light rail line connects the Mall of America and Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport in Bloomington to downtown,[554] and the Green Line travels from downtown through the University of Minnesota campus to downtown Saint Paul.[555] A Blue Line extension to the northwest suburbs is scheduled to be built and completed by 2030.[556] A Green Line extension is planned to connect downtown with the southwestern suburbs.[v] BRT lines are 25 percent faster than regular bus lines because riders pay before boarding, stops are limited, and sometimes they employ signal prioritization. Metro Transit plans to convert existing bus lines to BRT in the coming years.[558][559] In January 2026, bus service replaced the former Northstar Commuter rail from Big Lake, Minnesota, to downtown Minneapolis.[551]

A cyclist in winter

Hundreds of homeless people nightly sought shelter on Green Line trains until overnight service was cut back in 2019.[560] Short more than a hundred police officers, in 2022, the Metro Council hired community groups to help police light rail stations; these non-profits can guide passengers to mental health services and shelters.[561] In partnership with a private security company in 2024, Metro Transit improved security and safety with trip agents who ride the light rail lines each day and work with transit police and community officers[562]—as of 2026, 139 trip agents had cited about 0.2 percent of riders for nonpayment or other violations out of 2 million inspections.[563]

In 2007, the Interstate 35W bridge over the Mississippi, which was overloaded with 300 short tons (270,000 kg) of repair materials, collapsed, killing 13 people and injuring 145. The bridge was rebuilt in 14 months.[564]

Evie Carshare, owned by Minneapolis and Saint Paul since 2022, is a fleet of 145 electric cars available for one-way trips in a 35-square-mile (91 km2) area of the Twin Cities.[565] In warm weather, Lime and Veo have shared electric bikes and scooters for rent at sixty mobility hubs located on transit lines; riders may end their trip anywhere in the city.[566]

Minneapolis has 16 miles (26 km) of on-street protected bikeways, 98 miles (158 km) of bike lanes, and 101 miles (163 km) of off-street bikeways and trails.[567] Off-street facilities include the Grand Rounds National Scenic Byway, Midtown Greenway, Little Earth Trail, Hiawatha LRT Trail, Kenilworth Trail, and Cedar Lake Trail.[568] The Minneapolis Skyway System, 9.5 miles (15.3 km) of enclosed pedestrian bridges called skyways, links 80 city blocks downtown with access to second-floor restaurants, retailers, government, sports facilities, doctor's offices, and other businesses that are open on weekdays.[569] Fifteen commercial passenger airlines serve Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport (MSP).[570] MSP is the headquarters of Sun Country Airlines.[571] After it merged with Northwest Airlines in 2009, Delta Air Lines flew 80 percent of the airport's traffic,[572] and MSP was Delta's second-largest US hub.[573]

Services and utilitiesedit
A Downtown Improvement District ambassador

Xcel Energy supplies electricity,[574] and CenterPoint Energy provides gas.[574] The water supply is managed by four watershed districts that correspond with the Mississippi and three streams that are river tributaries.[575]

The city has nineteen fire stations.[576] Requests for non-emergency information or service requests can be made through Minneapolis 311. The call center operates in English, Spanish, Hmong, and Somali, and offers 220 language options.[577] Email, TTY, text, voice, and a mobile app can access the center.[578]

The Minneapolis department of public works is responsible for services including snow plowing, solid waste removal, traffic and parking, water treatment, transportation planning and maintenance, and fleet services for the city.[579] Among its engineering functions, the department was increasing the capacity of a 4,200-foot (1,300 m) storm water tunnel system 80 feet (24 m) under Washington to Chicago avenues and had completed 97 percent of the excavation phase and 41 percent of the lining phase as of August 2023.[580] Designed for downtown's concrete landscape, the system will drain runoff into the Mississippi in case of a 100-year storm.[581]

Downtown Improvement District ambassadors, who are identified by their blue-and-green-yellow fluorescent jackets, daily patrol a 120-block area of downtown to greet and assist visitors, remove trash, monitor property, and call police when they are needed. The ambassador program is a public-private partnership that is paid for by a special downtown tax district.[582]

Health careedit
See also: COVID-19 pandemic in Minnesota and COVID-19 pandemic in Minnesota § Economy
Hennepin County Medical Center has the state's busiest emergency room.[583]

Hennepin County Medical Center, a public teaching hospital and Level I trauma center,[584] opened in 1887 as City Hospital.[585] The city is also served by Abbott Northwestern Hospital, Children's Minnesota, and University of Minnesota and veterans medical centers.[586]

Cardiac surgery was developed at the University of Minnesota's Variety Club Heart Hospital.[587] Surgeon F. John Lewis successfully repaired a child's congenital heart defect in 1952.[588] By 1957, more than 200 patients—most of whom were children—had survived open-heart surgery.[589] Working with surgeon C. Walton Lillehei, Medtronic began to build portable and implantable cardiac pacemakers about this time.[590]

In 2022, opioid overdoses killed 231 persons in Minneapolis.[591] For the state in 2021, Black persons were three times and Native American persons were ten times more likely to die from an opioid overdose than White persons.[592][w] The 2024 city budget added funds for the Turning Point treatment center, which provides care specifically for African Americans.[207] The Red Lake Band of Chippewa is building a culturally sensitive treatment center for opioid and fentanyl addiction. Minneapolis transferred two city-owned properties to the Red Lake Nation for the facility.[594][595]

The Mashkiki Waakaa'igan Pharmacy—funded by the Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa—dispenses free prescription drugs and culturally sensitive care to members of any federally recognized tribes living in Hennepin and Ramsey counties, regardless of insurance status.[596]

 Because President Thomas Jefferson had not authorized Pike's trip, which was made at the behest of James Wilkinson, the new governor of the Louisiana territory, Pike did not have the authority to make a treaty.[31] Pike valued the land at $200,000 ($4.3 million in 2025)[32] in his journal but omitted the value in Article 2 of the treaty.  In the 1851 Treaty of Traverse des Sioux and Treaty of Mendota, the US took all Dakota land west of the Mississippi,[41] about 24 million acres (97,000 km2),[42] in exchange for a 10-mile (16 km) wide reservation on the Minnesota River[43] and about $3 million ($116 million in 2025).[32] After expenses, the Dakota were promised fifty years of annuities in goods[44] and interest on $1,360,000 ($52.6 million in 2025) and $1,410,000 ($54.6 million in 2025);[32] the US kept the principal.[45] The Dakota could not read English, and their interpreters worked for the US.[40] In Mendota, negotiator Wakute said he feared signing a treaty because the prior treaty was changed from the one he had signed.[46] The US Congress ratified amendments after the fact, and refused to consider payment unless the Dakota agreed to their new terms—in 1852 Congress struck the reservation from the final treaty.[47] Negotiators Luke Lea and Alexander Ramsey had promised the Dakota they would prosper, and they rushed the transaction.[48] The chiefs were asked to sign a third paper in 1851—onlookers assumed it was a third copy of the treaty[49]—that Ramsey later declared was a "solemn acknowledgment" of the Dakota's debt to traders.[50] Ramsey, as territorial governor, enforced the trader's paper, distributing the monies to himself, Henry Sibley, and their friends.[51]

 General[62] Henry Sibley rushed to complete the trials before winter.[63] Trials were held from late September[64] through early November 1862, in central Minnesota west of Minneapolis;[63] on each day up to forty-three men stood trial.[63] The Dakota men were without counsel, rarely spoke English, in some cases trials proceeded without witnesses, and no time was made for cross-examination.[65] Historian Gary Clayton Anderson says, "In 90 percent of the trials, the entire event lasted only a minute or two...".[65]
 Sibley appointed a commission of men thought later to be biased to hear the trials and planned to carry out executions immediately.[66] Of 400 Dakota, 303 were sentenced to death, 20 were sentenced to prison, 69 were acquitted, and 8 were released.[67] When his superior Major General John Pope reported the commission's findings to President Abraham Lincoln he had realized only the president can authorize executions. Historian Mary Lethert Wingerd writes that Lincoln and members of his cabinet were "taken aback" by the number of condemned and the irregular proceedings.[68] Lincoln then ordered a stay of execution until he could review the trial transcripts.[68] Minnesotans wanted revenge and many were outraged at the stay.[69] Lincoln was under pressure from Minnesotans,[70] and wrote that he wished to avoid cruelty and to discourage another outbreak.[71] He first decided that only rapists would be hanged, but only 2 Dakota met that condition. Then with the help of his lawyers,[72] Wingerd writes that Lincoln "reluctantly"[70] ordered that 39 men[73] would be hanged; these men had been convicted of murdering civilians. One received a last minute reprieve.[71] Minnesotans participated in lynch mobs and vigilantism against the Dakota, both condemned and friendly—2 men died of injuries sustained during attacks on Sibley's wagon train that took them to Mankato. Command transferred to Colonel Stephen Miller who oversaw the executions—he declared martial law and banned alcohol for the 4,000 spectators.[74] The Dakota were reportedly cheerful as they walked to their deaths; a journalist wrote, "No equal number ever approached the gallows with greater courage, and more perfect determination to prove how little death can be feared".[75] After what was the largest mass execution in US history,[76][75] Minnesota officials discovered that in their haste, they had hanged 2 innocent men.[71] Nearly all the men's bodies were dug up from their graves within 24 hours, some for trophies but most by physicians who wanted cadavers to dissect.[77]

# Trivia

## Lou Grant

Edit

Mrs. Pynchon, the widowed owner of the fictional Los Angeles Tribune, was based on [Katherine Graham](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm1200691/?ref_=tttrv_tr), the real widowed owner of the Washington Post, and on Dorothy "Dolly" Schiff, owner and publisher of the New York Post. For example, Schiff always carried her little dog with her, as Mrs. Pynchon does.

Helpful•32 0

The producers of the show wanted to air a final episode that dealt with the paper going out of business. They actually interviewed reporters from real newspapers that closed in order to prepare for this episode. The show was taken off the air before that episode could be filmed.

Helpful•30 0

When the series aired on CBS on Monday nights, journalism classes would dismiss early, so that the faculty and students could watch the new episodes, and discuss them in class.

Helpful•38 1

During the primetime run of the show (1977-1982), [Edward Asner](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000799/?ref_=tttrv_tr) became increasingly vocal on behalf of various liberal political causes. Although the series had slipped in ratings by 1982, many critics speculated that the actor's politics played a major role in the show's cancellation.

Helpful•35 2

A spin-off of the sitcom [The Mary Tyler Moore Show (1970)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0065314/?ref_=tttrv_tr), this is one of only two dramatic series in American television history to originate from a comedy series. The other was [Trapper John, M.D. (1979)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0078704/?ref_=tttrv_tr), which was a spin-off of [M*A*S*H (1972)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0068098/?ref_=tttrv_tr).

[](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000799/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_sm)

Edward Asner was born of Russian Jewish parentage in Kansas City, to Morris David Asner (founder and owner of the Kansas City-based Asner Iron & Metal Company) and his wife Elizabeth "Lizzie" (Seliger). After attending college, Ed worked various jobs, including in a steel mill, as a door-to-door salesman and on an assembly line for General Motors. Between 1947 and 1949, he attended the University of Chicago. The onset of the Korean War saw him drafted into the U.S. Army Signals Corps and posted to France where he was primarily assigned clerical tasks. Upon demobilization, Asner joined the Playwrights Theatre Company in Chicago but soon progressed to New York. In 1955, he appeared off-Broadway in the leading role of the beggar king Jonathan Peachum in Brecht's Threepenny Opera. Five years later, he made his debut on the Great White Way in the courtroom drama Face of a Hero, co-starring alongside [Jack Lemmon](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000493/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He also began regular TV work in anthology drama.  
  
From the early '60s, Asner, now based in California, earned his living as a busy supporting actor. His many noted guest appearances included turns in [Route 66 (1960)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0053534/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [The Untouchables (1959)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0052522/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [The Fugitive (1963)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0056757/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea (1964)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0057798/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) (sinister dictator-in-exile Brynov), [The Invaders (1967)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0061265/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) (twice -- as aliens) and [How the Ghosts Stole Christmas (1998)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0751138/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) (one of a couple of ghostly residents in a haunted mansion). Heavy-set and distinctively gravelly-voiced, Asner established his reputation as tough, robust and uncompromising (though, on occasion, good-hearted) authority figures. Excellent at conveying menace, he was memorably cast as the brutish patriarch Axel Jordache in [Rich Man, Poor Man (1976)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0074048/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and as the slave ship's morally conflicted master, Captain Thomas Davies, in [Roots (1977)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0075572/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), which earned him a Primetime Emmy Award in 1977. The immensely prolific Asner (417 IMDB screen credits!) would receive seven Emmys in total (from 21 nominations), all Primetime, and become the only actor to win in both the comedy and drama category for the same role. That was also the part which made Asner a household name: the gruff, snarky newspaper editor [Lou Grant (1977)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0075528/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). Grant began as a mainstay on [The Mary Tyler Moore Show (1970)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0065314/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), a 30-minute sitcom.  
  
When the character was promoted to West Coast editor of The Los Angeles Tribune, Asner went on to star in his own much acclaimed drama series. Despite consistently high ratings, the show was axed after five seasons amid rumours of disharmony between the star and producers, possibly due to the former's outspoken political views. Indeed, Asner has been a controversial figure as an activist and campaigner, engaged in a variety of humanitarian and political issues. A self-proclaimed liberal Democrat, he published a book in 2017, amusingly titled "The Grouchy Historian: An Old-Time Lefty Defends Our Constitution Against Right-Wing Hypocrites and Nutjobs."  
  
Between 1981 and 1985, Asner served twice as President of the Screen Actors Guild, during which time he was critical of former SAG President [Ronald Reagan](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0001654/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) -- then the president of a greater concern -- for his Central American policy. In 1996, he was inducted into the Television Hall of Fame and in 2002 received the Screen Actors Guild's Life Achievement Award. In addition to appearing on screen and stage, he performed extensive work for radio, video games and animated TV series. He voiced the lead character Carl Fredricksen in Pixar's Oscar-winning production of [Up (2009)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1049413/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), starred as Santa in [Elf (2003)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0319343/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), and played Nicholas Drago in [The Games Maker (2014)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2766268/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). Ed passed away in Los Angeles at the age of 91 on August 29, 2021.

**Eddie Asner**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-Tname-1) ([/ˈ æ z n ər/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); November 15, 1929 – August 29, 2021) was an American actor. He is most notable for portraying [Lou Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Grant "Lou Grant") on the sitcom _[The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mary\_Tyler\_Moore\_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show")_ (1970–1977) and drama _[Lou Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou\_Grant\_(TV\_series) "Lou Grant (TV series)")_ (1977–1982), making him one of the few television actors to portray the same character in both a comedy and a drama.

Asner won seven [Primetime Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Awards "Primetime Emmy Awards"), the most of any male performer. Five were for portraying Lou Grant: three as [Supporting Actor in a Comedy Television Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Supporting_Actor_in_a_Comedy_Series "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series") on _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_ and two as [Lead Actor in a Dramatic Television Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Lead_Actor_in_a_Drama_Series "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series") on the spin-off _Lou Grant_. The other two were for performances in the miniseries _[Rich Man, Poor Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rich\_Man,\_Poor\_Man\_(miniseries) "Rich Man, Poor Man (miniseries)")_ (1976) and _[Roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots\_(1977\_miniseries) "Roots (1977 miniseries)")_ (1977).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-cnn-2)

Asner acted in the films _[El Dorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Dorado\_(1966\_film) "El Dorado (1966 film)")_ (1966), _[They Call Me Mister Tibbs!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/They\_Call\_Me\_Mister\_Tibbs! "They Call Me Mister Tibbs!")_ (1970), _[Fort Apache, The Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort\_Apache,\_The\_Bronx "Fort Apache, The Bronx")_ (1981), _[JFK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK\_(film) "JFK (film)")_ (1991), and _[Too Big to Fail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too\_Big\_to\_Fail\_(film) "Too Big to Fail (film)")_ (2011). He also played [Santa Claus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Claus "Santa Claus") in several films and voiced [Carl Fredricksen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Fredricksen "Carl Fredricksen") in the [Pixar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixar "Pixar") animated film _[Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Up\_(2009\_film) "Up (2009 film)")_ (2009).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-3)

Asner starred in the [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") sitcom _[Thunder Alley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunder\_Alley\_(TV\_series) "Thunder Alley (TV series)")_ (1994–1995), and _[Michael: Every Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael:\_Every\_Day "Michael: Every Day")_ (2011–2017). He also acted extensively in numerous television series such as _[The Practice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Practice "The Practice")_, _[Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio\_60\_on\_the\_Sunset\_Strip "Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip")_, _[The Good Wife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Good\_Wife "The Good Wife")_, _[Cobra Kai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra\_Kai "Cobra Kai")_, _[Briarpatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Briarpatch\_(TV\_series) "Briarpatch (TV series)")_, _[Working Class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working\_Class\_(TV\_series) "Working Class (TV series)")_, and _[Dead to Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead\_to\_Me\_(TV\_series) "Dead to Me (TV series)")_. He also voiced [J. Jonah Jameson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Jonah_Jameson "J. Jonah Jameson") in _[Spider-Man: The Animated Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-Man:\_The\_Animated\_Series "Spider-Man: The Animated Series")_ (1994–1998), Hudson in _[Gargoyles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gargoyles\_(TV\_series) "Gargoyles (TV series)")_ (1994–1997), and Ed Wuncler Sr. in _[The Boondocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boondocks\_(TV\_series) "The Boondocks (TV series)")_ (2005–2014).

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Asner was born November 15, 1929,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-4) in [Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri"), and grew up in [Kansas City, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Kansas "Kansas City, Kansas").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-birthplace-5) His parents, Lizzie ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")Seliger; 1885–1967), a housewife, and Morris David Asner (1879–1957),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-6) were [Ashkenazi Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashkenazi_Jewish "Ashkenazi Jewish") immigrants from [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania") and [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") who ran a [second-hand shop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-hand_shop "Second-hand shop") and junkyard.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-birthplace-5) His four older siblings were Ben J. Asner (1915–1986), Eve Asner (1916–2014), Esther Edelman (1919–2014) and Labe Asner (1923–2017).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-NYT-7) He was raised in an [Orthodox Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthodox_Jewish "Orthodox Jewish") family and given the [Hebrew name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_name "Hebrew name") Yitzhak (יִצְחָק).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-Asner-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-9)

Asner attended [Wyandotte High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyandotte_High_School "Wyandotte High School") in Kansas City, Kansas, and the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"). He studied journalism in Chicago until a professor advised him there was little money to be made in the profession. He had been working in a steel mill,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-Palast-10) but he quickly switched to drama, debuting as the martyred [Thomas Becket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Becket "Thomas Becket") in a campus production of [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot")'s _[Murder in the Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder\_in\_the\_Cathedral "Murder in the Cathedral")_. He eventually dropped out of school, going to work as a taxi driver, worked on the assembly line for [General Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Motors "General Motors"), and other odd jobs before being drafted in the military in 1951.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-11)

Asner served with the [United States Army Signal Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Signal_Corps "United States Army Signal Corps") from 1951 to 1953 during the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War") and appeared in plays that toured army bases in Europe.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-12)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-NYT-7)

### 1955–1969: Early work and television roles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1955–1969: Early work and television roles")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1970.jpg/250px-Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1970.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1970.jpg)

Cast of _[The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mary\_Tyler\_Moore\_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show")_ in 1970, with Asner in center rear

Following his military service, Asner helped found the Playwrights Theatre Company in Chicago, but left for [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") before members of that company regrouped as the [Compass Players](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass_Players "Compass Players") in the mid-1950s.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-eb-13) He later made frequent guest appearances with the successor to Compass, [The Second City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Second_City "The Second City").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-14) In New York City, [Off-Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-Broadway "Off-Broadway") roles included Jonathan Jeremiah Peachum in the revival of _[Threepenny Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Threepenny\_Opera "The Threepenny Opera")_ and in Otway's [Venice Preserv'd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Preserv'd "Venice Preserv'd") in late 1955.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-15) Asner scored his first [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") role in _Face of a Hero_ alongside [Jack Lemmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Lemmon "Jack Lemmon") in 1960, and began to make inroads as a television actor, having made his TV debut in 1957 on _[Studio One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westinghouse\_Studio\_One "Westinghouse Studio One")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-cnn-2) In two notable performances on television, Asner played Detective Sgt. Thomas Siroleo in the 1963 episode of _[The Outer Limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Outer\_Limits\_(1963\_TV\_series) "The Outer Limits (1963 TV series)")_ titled "[It Crawled Out of the Woodwork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It_Crawled_Out_of_the_Woodwork "It Crawled Out of the Woodwork")" and the reprehensible ex-premier Brynov in the 1965 _[Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyage\_to\_the\_Bottom\_of\_the\_Sea\_(TV\_series) "Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea (TV series)")_ episode "The Exile". He made his film debut in 1962, in the [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley "Elvis Presley") vehicle _[Kid Galahad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid\_Galahad "Kid Galahad")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-cnn-2)

Before landing his role with [Mary Tyler Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mary_Tyler_Moore_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show"), Asner guest-starred in television series including four episodes of _[The Untouchables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Untouchables\_(1959\_TV\_series) "The Untouchables (1959 TV series)")_ starring [Robert Stack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stack "Robert Stack"), the [syndicated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_syndication "Television syndication")[crime drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_drama "Crime drama")_[Decoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decoy\_(TV\_series) "Decoy (TV series)")_, starring [Beverly Garland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Garland "Beverly Garland"), two episodes of _[Naked City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naked\_City\_(TV\_series) "Naked City (TV series)")_ in 1961, and _[Route 66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Route\_66\_(TV\_series) "Route 66 (TV series)")_ in 1962 (the episode titled "Welcome to the Wedding") as Custody Officer Lincoln Peers. He was cast on [Jack Lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Lord "Jack Lord")'s [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") drama series _[Stoney Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoney\_Burke\_(TV\_series) "Stoney Burke (TV series)")_ and in the series finale of [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS")'s _[The Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Reporter\_(TV\_series) "The Reporter (TV series)")_, starring [Harry Guardino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Guardino "Harry Guardino"). He also appeared on _[Mr. Novak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_Novak "Mr. Novak")_, _[Ben Casey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben\_Casey "Ben Casey")_, _[Gunsmoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunsmoke "Gunsmoke")_, _[Mission: Impossible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission:\_Impossible\_(1966\_TV\_series) "Mission: Impossible (1966 TV series)")_, _[The Outer Limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Outer\_Limits\_(1963\_TV\_series) "The Outer Limits (1963 TV series)")_, _[The Fugitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fugitive\_(1963\_TV\_series) "The Fugitive (1963 TV series)")_, and _[The Invaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Invaders "The Invaders")_. In 1963, Asner appeared as George Johnson on _[The Virginian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Virginian\_(TV\_series) "The Virginian (TV series)")_ in the episode "Echo of Another Day".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-16) In 1968 he was the villain Furman Crotty in the Wild Wild West episode "The Night of the Amnesiac".

### 1970–1982: _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_ and _Lou Grant_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1970–1982: The Mary Tyler Moore Show and Lou Grant")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1977.jpg/250px-Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1977.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1977.jpg)

Publicity photo of the cast of [The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mary_Tyler_Moore_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show") in 1977. From left standing: [Ted Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Knight "Ted Knight") (Ted Baxter), [Gavin McLeod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_McLeod "Gavin McLeod") (Murray Slaughter), Ed Asner (Lou Grant). Seated: [Betty White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_White "Betty White") (Sue Ann Nivens), [Georgia Engel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Engel "Georgia Engel") (Georgette Baxter), [Mary Tyler Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Tyler_Moore "Mary Tyler Moore") (Mary Richards).

Asner was best known for his character [Lou Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Grant "Lou Grant"), who was first introduced on _[The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mary\_Tyler\_Moore\_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show")_ in 1970. In 1977, after Moore's series ended, Asner's character was given his own show, _[Lou Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou\_Grant\_(TV\_series) "Lou Grant (TV series)")_ (1977–82). In contrast to the _Mary Tyler Moore_ series, a thirty-minute award-winning comedy about television journalism, the _Lou Grant_ series was an hour-long award-winning drama about newspaper journalism. For his role as Grant, Asner was one of only two actors to win an Emmy Award for a sitcom and a drama for the same role (the second being [Uzo Aduba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uzo_Aduba "Uzo Aduba")). In addition he made appearances as Lou Grant on two other shows: _[Rhoda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhoda "Rhoda")_ and _[Roseanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseanne "Roseanne")_.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-17) Other television series starring Asner in regular roles include _[Thunder Alley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunder\_Alley\_(TV\_series) "Thunder Alley (TV series)")_, _[The Bronx Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bronx\_Zoo\_(TV\_series) "The Bronx Zoo (TV series)")_, and _[Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio\_60\_on\_the\_Sunset\_Strip "Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip")_. He also starred in one episode of the [Western series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westerns_on_television "Westerns on television")_[Dead Man's Gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead\_Man's\_Gun "Dead Man's Gun")_ (1997), as well as portraying art smuggler August March in an episode of the original _[Hawaii Five-O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii\_Five-O\_(1968\_TV\_series) "Hawaii Five-O (1968 TV series)")_ (1975) and reprised the role in the _[Hawaii Five-0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii\_Five-0\_(2010\_TV\_series) "Hawaii Five-0 (2010 TV series)")_ (2012) remake.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-18) He also appeared as a streetwise veteran police officer in an episode of the 1973 version of _[Police Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_(1973\_TV\_series) "Police Story (1973 TV series)")_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-19)

Asner was acclaimed for his role in the ABC miniseries _[Roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots\_(1977\_miniseries) "Roots (1977 miniseries)")_, as Captain Davies, the morally conflicted captain of the _Lord Ligonier_, the slave ship that brought [Kunta Kinte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunta_Kinte "Kunta Kinte") to America.
